articles.title: Air Rifles
articles.body: Spring / gas-ram air rifles: cheaper guns, cheaper pellets. With cartridge prices rising, air rifles are among the first practical alternatives — cheaper guns, cheaper pellets. This opener covers spring / gas-ram designs, how they work, and why they demand respect. After our discussion of rising cartridge prices and available alternatives, it is worth noting that one of the first practical options is hunting with air rifles — for their relative affordability and that of their pellets. We begin with air rifles in their many types, shapes, and sizes: what they share, what sets each type apart, and how the firing system shapes performance. In a series of articles we will cover each type, its weak points, and the advantages and drawbacks of each design. The best-known air-rifle type is the spring / gas-ram airgun. What made it so widespread is availability and an acceptable price, putting it within everyone’s reach; most hunters owned one at the start of their path. How the rifle works — brief overview: Opening the barrel (“break barrel”) or using a tool or handle under the barrel (“underlever”). In both types above, the purpose of the handle or barrel action is to compress the spring or piston so that air is compressed in the storage chamber inside the rifle body. When the trigger is pressed, the spring or piston is released, and with it the compressed air in the reservoir, driving the projectile. The pellet leaves the barrel with a spiral (rifled) spin. When the trigger is pressed, the spring or piston is released. Many believe that a piston- or spring-powered air rifle is inaccurate. That is wrong: there are very accurate rifles, but one must always choose high-quality guns. Among the drawbacks of this system is that the shooter must practise thoroughly because of barrel vibration; that vibration varies and affects accuracy depending on how the rifle is held and handled. The rifle is very sensitive to hold and practice — the only way to reach satisfactory accuracy. It is worth noting that air rifles have hunting limitations; chief among them is that take is on perched birds, with its own challenges — challenges that add an extra pleasure to the hunt. Air-rifle pellets remain relatively affordable. Will we see a rush toward air rifles in the near future? Will the scene shift from 12-gauge and .410 shotguns to air guns? Next season will tell us everything. We stress: air rifles are very dangerous. Everyone must be responsible and treat them as firearms — they must never be underestimated.

articles.title: From the Atlas Foothills to the Red Sea Coast… The Arab Hunting Season Enters Autumn 2026
articles.body: A group of hunters and their dogs advancing on a dirt track through Atlas scrub — a Maghreb field scene from Morocco’s foothills.حجل أطلس / Hajal Atlas Guns return to some open country and stay silent in others… Nine Arab states meet the autumn migration with nine different hunting maps With the first shift in the late-summer air, a scene every Arab hunter knows begins to form. From the Atlas foothills in Morocco and Algeria, through Tunisia’s woodlands, Libya’s coasts, and Egypt’s marshes, then along the great eastern flyway through Lebanon, Syria, and Jordan, out to the deserts of Saudi Arabia and the Red Sea shore, birds move south—and with them moves the memory of a whole season of waiting. This is migration autumn. It is not, necessarily, hunting autumn everywhere. As October 2026 begins, the Arab hunting map looks like a mosaic of systems, dates, and limits: Saudi Arabia entered its season at the start of September; Jordan opened defined seasons for named species; Morocco and Tunisia opened their seasons on 4 October, while Algeria set 10 October as the official opening date under each wilaya’s approved hunting plan; in Lebanon, wild hunting remains closed because no official open-season decision has been issued. And in Libya, autumn itself brought the opposite kind of decree in parts of the southeast: protect migrants and ban hunting them. So the journey from the Atlas to the Red Sea is not only a journey between countries. It is a journey between wholly different ways of handling hunting, migration, and wildlife. Morocco: the first Sunday in October returns hunters to the field On the Atlas slopes, among forests and plains that shaped one of North Africa’s deepest hunting cultures, the season has begun. Morocco’s 2026–2027 hunting season opened nationwide on Sunday, 4 October 2026, the date set by the Higher Council for Hunting. The decision followed an assessment of the 2025–2026 season and the state of the national game stock, within a policy that ties continued hunting to managing species and habitats. According to the National Agency for Water and Forests (ANEF) report published on 6 October, the first day’s national average bag was 1.91 partridges per hunter, with reinforced monitoring, awareness and guidance across hunting areas. Morocco is not a small hunting market. Last season, more than 65,000 hunters practised in open and leased domains, plus about five thousand in tourist hunting. That figure explains part of the scene that returns with every opening: hunting associations, hounds, partridge, leased and prepared land, and a standing tourist-hunting sector that receives shooters from abroad. But 4 October does not make every bird fair game. The annual decision sets species, periods, and bags; turtle dove stays outside the general opening and keeps its own seasonal calendar. From here the journey turns east. Hunter and pointing dog in Atlas scrub — shotgun on the shoulder, cartridge belt, mountain woodland.حجل أطلس / Hajal Atlas Algeria: a national opening on 10 October, implementation under each wilaya’s plan The Directorate General of Forests announced the official opening of the 2026–2027 hunting season from Saturday, 10 October 2026, under each wilaya’s approved hunting plan, in a statement reported by the Algerian Press Service (APS) on 30 September. The statement requires compliance with the hunting areas defined in the plan, excluding fire-affected areas, and with the permitted species, hunting periods and quotas. For the hunter, knowing the national opening date is not enough; the questions remain: In which wilaya? For which quarry? Within which areas, periods and quotas? From northern forests to the high plateaus, the local decision becomes part of the hunter’s kit—alongside gun and dog. That a species may be hunted in one place does not make it lawful somewhere else. Tunisia: also 4 October… but on a densely detailed calendar Across the Algerian border, the picture is clearer. Tunisia’s Ministry of Agriculture, Water Resources and Fisheries issued its decision regulating the 2026–2027 season, published in the Official Gazette. On 4 October 2026, hunting of hare, partridge, resident quail, rock dove, and sandgrouse (“kudra”) opened and runs to 6 December, limited to Sundays, public holidays, and official leave days. Waterbirds keep another clock. Woodpigeon and a wide set of waterfowl do not open until 22 November 2026, running to 28 March 2027. The list includes ducks, teal, geese, coot and others, with special rules for waterbird hunting on “the pass.” This detail states a principle that repeats across the Arab map: migration does not open the season; the legal decision does. The sky may fill with birds long before the law allows a single shot. Migration is not a hunting permit A sky full of birds does not make a shot legal. A season opens by official decision—species, place, time, bag—not by the migration calendar alone. Two hunters on a Moroccan slope aiming shotguns amid green brush under a clear sky.حجل أطلس / Hajal Atlas Libya: autumn arrives this time with a protection order Farther east, the scene grows more complex. In Libya—where desert, wetlands, and coastal corridors form parts of the Europe–Africa flyways—September 2026 brought news unlike the usual season openings. On 20 September, the Libyan Authority for Heritage and Wildlife announced a ban on hunting migratory birds in several southeastern areas after declines in numbers and hunting practices described as wrongful and abusive. The measure covered Jalu, Awjila and Jikhra (Ijkhira) and other zones out to Tazirbu and Kufra, protecting the natural corridors linked to them, for two consecutive migration seasons (passage and return). So while Moroccan and Tunisian hunters returned to the field on 4 October, a hunter in parts of Libya faces a different sign: birds pass here, but passage is not permission. It is one of the sharpest paradoxes of the Arab 2026 season. Egypt: when quail reach the coast Then the road reaches Egypt. Here autumn is visible on the Mediterranean shore, in the Delta, and on the northern lakes. Quail, garganey and other migratory birds make Egypt one of the known stops on the Eurasia–Africa flyway. In September 2026, the 2026–2027 bird-hunting season had already opened within the legal hunting frame—including wild quail, garganey, and other species expressly authorized under the governing ministerial decree. Turtle dove is not listed here among the expressly authorized species. The message that accompanied the start was plain: opening the season is not opening hunting without limits. Some species are allowed, others protected; practice is regulated; the stated aim is to keep hunting possible without turning the yearly migration into depletion. Egypt especially shows how hard that balance is. Its position makes it a vast geographic bridge for migrants—from the Mediterranean coast and Lake Bardawil to the Delta, Fayoum, and beyond. Here the line between the lawful hunter and random shooting is more than wording; it is the difference between a season that can return and a resource that can vanish. Lebanon: the birds arrived… but the season did not open A Lebanese hunter with a shotgun on a mountain ridge under the autumn sky. From Egypt to the eastern Mediterranean, we reach the most sensitive case. Lebanon sits on one of the region’s major bird-migration corridors. In autumn large numbers of migrants cross its skies. But as of 29 September 2026, no official decision has opened the 2026–2027 wild-hunting season. Wild hunting therefore remains prohibited until the legal decision that opens the season is issued. This is not theory. On 14 September the Internal Security Forces announced the arrest of three people in Danniyeh as part of efforts against abusive wild hunting and for protecting migratory birds. Lebanon’s terrestrial hunting law No. 580 of 2004 provides that opening and closing the season, and the quarry list, fall to the Minister of Environment on a proposal from the Higher Council for Hunting; the season does not open automatically with the arrival of autumn. So a Lebanese hunter may see autumn flocks over mountains and valleys, yet quarry overhead does not make a season. The law does. Syria: birds return before the regulatory picture is complete Northward, migrants cross Syrian land—from the coast to inland plains and wetlands. Scattered field reports point to ongoing terrestrial hunting in some areas, alongside crackdowns on illegal hunting elsewhere, without that translating into a clear published national calendar for autumn 2026–2027. As of late September 2026, the published regulatory picture remains incomplete: no recent, reliable central decision has set a national Syrian calendar for autumn 2026–2027 with the clarity available for Morocco, Tunisia, or Saudi Arabia. Hunting on the ground is one thing; a published legal season with limits, species, and dates is another. What has not been published officially stays outside the confirmed calendar map. Jordan: ten birds per outing… and partridge stays closed In Jordan the precise numbers return. On 18 September 2026 an autumn season opened for defined pigeon species, running to 29 November, on Fridays and Sundays only, in permitted areas west of the Hejaz railway. The Wildlife Protection Committee set a ceiling of 10 pigeons of the allowed species per licensed hunter per outing, excluding the European turtle dove (Streptopelia turtur), known locally as al-hamam al-raqti, according to Jordanian reporting of the RSCN announcement on 17 September. Most important: opening pigeons did not become a general open season. The committee kept partridge and sand partridge closed. Call devices and nets are banned, night hunting is banned, and a licence plus compliance with permitted zones are required. Jordan: open by species, not by blank season Pigeons: 18 Sep–29 Nov · Fri & Sun · west of Hejaz railway · max 10/outing (European turtle dove excluded). Partridge & sand partridge closed. ʿUṣfūr al-tīn & al-farr: 15 Aug–31 Oct · 15 each/outing. Callers, nets, night hunting banned. Jordan had also opened an autumn season for the birds known locally as ʿuṣfūr al-tīn (Eurasian blackcap, Sylvia atricapilla—«fig sparrow» in Levant hunting speech) and al-farr (local name; scientific identity not locked in official English wording) from 15 August through 31 October 2026, at 15 birds of each species per licensed hunter per outing in defined areas. It is a model of opening by species, period, bag, and place—not an unbounded “season is open.” Saudi Arabia: from 1 September… a sixth season into midwinter At the eastern end of the journey, the map reaches the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Here the season began ahead of most countries we have passed. The National Center for Wildlife Development officially announced the sustainable hunting season 2026–2027 starting 1 September 2026 and running to 31 January 2027. The present season is the sixth since the regulatory experiment began in 2021. Permitted species rose to 30, with the national bag up 11% and licences up 34%, according to the Center. In the autumn window, from September through the end of November, the list includes species such as common quail, common partridge, sand partridge, and a range of pigeons, doves, and sandgrouse, among others; some species are taken with falcons. But the Saudi picture differs sharply from the classic Arab image of a hunter with a shotgun. The current system allows licensed non-powder hunting guns powered by gas or spring pressure, plus falconry under its rules, and bans pellet guns, nets, and unauthorised attraction or calling devices. The hunter also needs a permit through the “Fitri” platform. The spatial limit is striking too: hunting is barred inside reserves, major projects, populated areas and other defined zones, and along the Kingdom’s coasts to a depth of 20 kilometres inland. Saudi: “Fitri” permit + 20 km coastal ban Sixth season (1 Sep 2026–31 Jan 2027) · 30 species · via Fitri. Licensed non-powder guns (gas/spring) + falconry under rules; pellet guns, nets, unauthorised callers banned. No hunting in reserves, populated zones, or along coasts 20 km inland. Here, at the Red Sea, the journey ends. One sky… nine different seasons From the Atlas to the Red Sea, birds do not know the borders people drew. The quail leaving the northern Mediterranean carries no passport. Pigeons, ducks, and passage birds do not know whether the sky below is Moroccan, Tunisian, Egyptian, or Jordanian. But the hunter knows—or must. Autumn 2026 shows a clear shift in what an “Arab season” means. The question is no longer only “Has hunting started?” but what may be taken, where, when, by what means, and in what number. Morocco and Tunisia opened their seasons on 4 October. Saudi Arabia entered on 1 September under a system of licences, bags, and species. Jordan opened some species and closed others. Egypt met migration season within legally regulated hunting. Algeria set Saturday, 10 October as the official opening date, with implementation governed by each wilaya’s approved hunting plan. In parts of Libya, the season arrived as protection and prohibition. In Lebanon, through the end of September, the season had not opened at all. As for Syria, the published regulatory picture remains less clear as of late September, with no confirmed national calendar in the available official sources. Nine countries, then—and nine hunting maps under one autumn sky. Perhaps the most important change a hunter should read in 2026–2027 is this: the survival of hunting no longer hinges only on quarry being present, but on hunters and authorities together keeping that quarry present for the season after. A lawful shot is not merely a shot fired inside the season dates. It is a shot that knows species, bag, place, and time. From Morocco’s Atlas foothills to Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea approaches, the future of Arab hunting looks set to be decided at those four edges.

articles.title: Arabian Saluki Center marks 25 years of preserving the falconer’s companion
articles.body: The Arabian Saluki Center building in Abu Dhabi. Founded in Abu Dhabi in 2001, the center combines Saluki care and training with the preservation of native Arabian bloodlines. Abu Dhabi’s Arabian Saluki Center is marking its 25th anniversary in 2026. Established in 2001 as a project of the Emirates Falconers’ Club, it has combined the preservation of hunting heritage with the development of care, training and native Arabian bloodline conservation. Over a quarter of a century, its work has expanded from boarding and daily care to breeding programs, bloodline documentation and veterinary services, alongside guidance for breeders and owners on care and responsible ownership. Training is a central part of this work. According to the club’s report, the center has running areas attached to its kennels and an outdoor training ground covering more than 1,000 square meters. Its programs include fitness, swimming, behavior, obedience and sprint racing, as well as preparation for shows and beauty competitions. One milestone has been its organization of the Arabian Saluki Beauty Contest at the Abu Dhabi International Hunting and Equestrian Exhibition since 2004. These activities continue with the 2026–2027 Arabian Saluki Championship in Al Ain and Al Dhafra, with competition expected to begin this November. The center also provides veterinary examinations and consultations, vaccinations and microchipping, together with travel and transport guidance. These practical services connect the preservation of the falconer’s companion with the needs of breeders and dogs today. Source: Emirates Falconers’ Club. articles.title: Arabian Saluki Championship starts in November with three distances and five season titles
articles.body: Salukis racing on a sandy track; a photograph supplied with the club’s press material. The Emirates Falconers’ Club and Abu Dhabi’s Arabian Saluki Centre will hold the inaugural season in Al Ain and Al Dhafra from November 2026 to April 2027. The Emirates Falconers’ Club and the Arabian Saluki Centre in Abu Dhabi will organise the first Arabian Saluki Championship in Al Ain and Al Dhafra from November 2026 to April 2027, aiming to develop this heritage sport and preserve its ties to hunting culture and desert life. The championship brings together speed, distance and endurance races in a season built around registration, classification and cumulative points. Handlers with Salukis in a photograph supplied with the club’s press material. Three distances for males and females Competitions comprise 1,000-metre sprints, 1,500-metre middle-distance races and 2,000-metre endurance races, with male and female categories. The season includes preliminary rounds, semi-finals and finals, with points accumulated across rounds to determine the category champions. Five seasonal titles will be awarded: Speed Champion, Distance Champion, Endurance Champion, Arabian Saluki Champion and Best Breeder. The programme also includes cash prizes, an Arabian Saluki beauty competition, or mazayen, and a simulated hunting competition using a mechanical lure. A registry of bloodlines, owners and breeders The club says the championship will establish the first official Arabian Saluki registry in the UAE and the Gulf region, documenting bloodlines, owners and breeders and issuing annual registration and classification certificates. The system will allow each Saluki’s performance to be tracked and assessed throughout the season rather than through a single race result. The organisers’ vision also includes a scientific database to study genetic and physical capabilities, programmes to improve bloodlines, training and assessment, and broader participation by owners, breeders and enthusiasts. Source: Emirates Falconers’ Club. Photographs: Emirates Falconers’ Club.

articles.title: Bearded Reedling
articles.body: Bearded Reedling Panurus biarmicus Identity and names Bearded Reedling, Panurus biarmicus, is Panure à moustaches in French and also known as Bearded Tit. Despite that alternative English name and Arabic names referring to a tit, it belongs to Panuridae, not the true-tit family Paridae. Its total length is about 14–17 cm, including a conspicuous long tail, and it weighs around 15 g. A small, rounded body combined with that tail creates a silhouette unlike most brown reedbed birds. Identification The male has a blue-grey head and black drooping moustachial marks beside a pale throat, above a largely cinnamon-brown body. The famous facial feature is therefore closer to moustaches than a beard. Females are plainer and lack those black marks; juveniles may show a black patch on the back. Wings are short and the bill compact. A long tail alone is insufficient: combine body shape, facial pattern, behaviour and habitat, especially during brief views between moving reed stems. Habitat, food and behaviour Extensive dense reedbeds are its characteristic habitat. Birds climb stems, disappear through vegetation and occasionally emerge on seed heads. Insects, larvae and other invertebrates feature strongly during warmer months, while seeds, including reed seeds, become more important in winter. Small swallowed grit particles help the gizzard process plant food; they are not a substitute for nourishment. Short ringing calls may reveal birds before they become visible. Understanding the reedbed itself is essential to interpreting their presence. Range and Arab occurrence Distribution is patchy across Europe and Asia, following suitable reeds, and Arab occurrence varies sharply. Published Syrian evidence includes fledged young at Sed Wadi Abied in August 1998 and resident breeding populations in suitable Euphrates and Jabbul reedbeds. These are historical, site-based records, not a current census of all Syria. Lebanon’s 2026 guide instead treats it as a vagrant, citing six at Aammiq in March 1996 and two at Anjar in April 2005. It is not a regular winter visitor to every Levantine wetland. Breeding and development The pair builds a cup nest among tangled vegetation low above water or mud. BTO gives a usual clutch of 4–8 eggs, shared incubation of about 10–14 days and fledging around 12–13 days after hatching. Chicks hatch helpless and need feeding and protection; care continues after nest departure. Further broods may follow in a suitable season, but water, vegetation and weather affect success. European breeding months should not automatically be transferred to an individual Arab locality. November and responsible observation In November, birds may gather in flocks and move among reed patches within their range, with occasional wider dispersal. Listening from an existing wetland edge is preferable to opening a new route through reeds. Record numbers, location and vegetation, seeking photographs of face and tail without playback to draw birds out. A possible Lebanese observation needs careful documentation rather than an immediate claim of new residence. Conversely, failure to see birds during a windy visit does not demonstrate disappearance. Conservation Its global category is Least Concern, but specialisation ties its future to healthy wetlands. Drainage, degradation, disturbance and lost cover can reduce usable habitat. Reed management must consider breeding and roosting places and their seasons instead of clearing a large area indiscriminately. Protecting water and connected cover benefits other wetland species too. A male’s attractive appearance never justifies approaching a nest or cutting stems for a cleaner photograph; safeguarding habitat matters more than the image. articles.title: From Dubai to a $2 million race… Bin Harmash takes inspiration from Japan
articles.body: Dark Saffron Dark Saffron prepares for the Breeders’ Cup Sprint at Keeneland on 31 October. Trainer Ahmad bin Harmash is drawing inspiration from the success of Japanese horses in American racing as he prepares for a new challenge with Dark Saffron, a two-time Dubai Golden Shaheen winner. Owned by Sultan Ali, the horse is preparing to contest the Breeders’ Cup Sprint at Keeneland on 31 October, an international Grade 1 dirt race over approximately 1,200 metres with a total purse of $2 million. In comments reported by Sean Collins, Bin Harmash wondered whether a team from another country could repeat the Japanese success. He explained that preparations began in late May and that the horse had settled well at Keeneland. articles.title: Birds in Bags… From an Akkar Sparrowhawk to Forged Trafficking Papers
articles.body: A sparrowhawk inside a backpack during an anti-poaching operation in Akkar, October 2026. In the highlands of Akkar, a backpack held an unexpected cargo: a sparrowhawk. One of two men detained by security forces was carrying the bird inside his bag during a field operation against the hunting of birds of prey, announced by the Committee Against Bird Slaughter, CABS, on 6 October 2026. The incident took place in a mountainous area of Akkar, following surveillance by CABS in cooperation with the Middle East Centre for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching, MECSHAP, and the security forces. According to the organisation, both men were taken to the police station, their weapons were confiscated and legal proceedings were initiated against them. The backpack is the detail that stays with the reader: a bird of prey, whose domain should be the sky, concealed among belongings carried on someone’s back. The published information does not establish that the Akkar incident was part of cross-border trade. It does, however, open a window onto other, separate cases in which concealing a bird is the beginning of the story, followed by an attempt to conceal its origins. In Spain… A Backpack Becomes Part of a Court Case On 14 October, SEO/BirdLife announced that it had joined criminal proceedings as a private prosecutor before Investigating Court No. 11 in Málaga, in the case arising from Operation Bétula. The investigation concerns suspected theft of raptor chicks from their nests, trafficking and forged documentation. Its participation marks a new legal development in a case whose underlying events took place months earlier. The operation was announced on 20 July 2026. According to the published account, two sparrowhawk chicks without identification rings were found inside a backpack in a car near Alhaurín el Grande, together with ten metal rings. The investigation examined whether wild-caught birds were being presented as captive-bred. Here, the backpack is no longer the only object under scrutiny. A ring attached to a bird’s leg and the document accompanying it are supposed to help establish its identity and origin. If they are used to misrepresent that origin, the appearance of legality itself becomes part of the case. The inquiry included checks on documents associated with CITES, the convention regulating international trade in endangered species, and the collection of samples for genetic tests to verify parentage. Collecting samples does not mean that test results have been issued, just as an investigation is not a conviction. There was another chapter in the two chicks’ story: coverage of the operation reported that the Guardia Civil’s mountain rescue team returned them to their nest. Questions about the origins of other birds and their accompanying documents remained before investigators. Goldfinches Bound for Oran About a month before the legal development in Málaga, a different case emerged at the Spanish port of Alicante. On 11 September 2026, details were published of the seizure of 1,500 goldfinches inside a car preparing to board a ferry to Oran, Algeria. According to information attributed to the Guardia Civil, the birds were packed into thirty boxes in severely overcrowded conditions, without the required documents. That large number conceals a loss that matters just as much: the reports said that 90 birds were found dead, another 90 needed care and 1,320 were released. Ninety goldfinches had paid the price before the sea crossing even began. In Akkar, a bird inside a backpack; in Alicante, hundreds of birds inside a car. The circumstances and numbers differ, but turning a living creature into concealed cargo puts it at risk before it reaches any market. Another Bag at Baghdad Airport Earlier in the year, on 2 January 2026, Video News Agency carried a statement from Iraq’s General Customs Authority about a live falcon discovered concealed in an Iraqi passenger’s bag at Baghdad International Airport’s Babylon arrivals hall. The passenger had arrived from the United Arab Emirates. The report referred to a single falcon and did not identify its species. That detail was absent from the information released about the seizure. These sources provide no evidence that the three cases were the work of a single network. What links them in this account is the method of concealment, and the questions each raises about the bird’s origins, its papers and the legality of possessing or transporting it. Earlier Cases Along the Same Route Goldfinch seizures are not new to Alicante’s port. SEO/BirdLife has cited the seizure of 83 goldfinches there in June 2025, also bound for Algeria. Earlier still, in 2022, around 2,400 goldfinches intended to be smuggled to Algeria were seized in Oujda, Morocco, according to the organisation’s account. These older incidents help explain why goldfinches recur in discussions of trade across the Mediterranean and within North Africa, without making every seizure evidence of an organised connection to those that preceded it. Tunisia: Seeking a Response Across Borders Against this backdrop, Tunisia is hosting an international meeting from 16 to 18 October 2026 to combat the illegal hunting, capture and trade of wild birds. According to an announcement by the Association Les Amis des Oiseaux, reported by Tunisian National Radio, the meeting brings together ten partners from eight Mediterranean countries. The programme focuses on sharing experience and improving monitoring, documentation and cooperation, particularly between North Africa and the Balkans. The Association Les Amis des Oiseaux and its partners are involved in organising the meeting, alongside institutions working to protect birds and natural habitats. The meeting’s importance becomes clear when these cases are considered together: field surveillance stops an offence, an inspection prevents a shipment from leaving, and an investigation looks beyond a ring or a document. Each step has a role, but protecting a bird does not end when it is taken out of a bag. A backpack may be opened in Akkar, a car at a Spanish port or luggage at Baghdad airport. The question remains open: when will bird smuggling and the illegal trade in birds end? Sources: CABS · SEO/BirdLife · Bétula · Málaga Hoy · Diario de Alicante · SEO/BirdLife · 1,500 · Video News Agency · Radio Nationale Tunisienne. Photo: Anti-Poaching Unit (APU).
articles.excerpt: A sparrowhawk concealed in Lebanon, two chicks that exposed a case in Spain, and goldfinches intercepted before crossing the Mediterranean. Separate incidents raise fresh questions about protecting birds, as a forgery case moves through…

articles.title: Black-headed Gull
articles.body: Black-headed Gull Chroicocephalus ridibundus Identity and identification Black-headed Gull Chroicocephalus ridibundus belongs to Laridae; older references use Larus ridibundus. The breeding hood is chocolate-brown. In winter it disappears, usually leaving a dark ear spot. Adults have reddish bills and legs. Habitat and food It uses coasts, estuaries, lakes and fields. Food includes invertebrates, small fish and items collected on land. A bird on a beach is not necessarily restricted to marine habitats. Breeding and development Colonies occupy vegetation or low ground, often near water. BTO gives a typical clutch of 2–3 eggs, shared incubation of 23–26 days and fledging at about 34–36 days. Before flight, chicks still depend on parental protection and feeding. Arab occurrence and seasonality Lebanon’s 2020 checklist describes abundant passage and winter presence from August to late April, peaking in November and December. Qatar’s current list calls it a common winter visitor. November offers a useful lesson in recognising winter plumage despite the species’ name. Observation and conservation Clean water and undisturbed resting areas matter. Its abundance should not be transferred to other gull species, and gathering near rubbish does not remove its need for natural habitat. articles.title: Black Kite
articles.body: Black Kite Milvus migrans Identity and identification Black Kite Milvus migrans belongs to Accipitridae. Brown and long-winged, it has a shallowly forked tail that can look square when spread. Juveniles are more spotted. Compared with Red Kite, the tail is shorter and less deeply forked. Some references split Yellow-billed Kite, whereas AviList 2026 includes it within M. migrans pending further research. It is placed in the order Accipitriformes. Habitat, food and behaviour Open country, water, urban edges and sites with prey or carrion provide food. It takes fish, small animals and scraps and may steal from other birds. Large gatherings at a dump demonstrate food concentration, not necessarily safe food or healthy habitat. Breeding and parental care A twig nest usually stands in a tree, sometimes on rock, and may incorporate collected lining material. Two or three eggs are usual; incubation lasts about a month. Chicks require roughly six to eight weeks before flight and further care afterwards. Details vary geographically. Range and Arab occurrence Widespread in the Old World, it includes resident and migratory populations. Lebanon’s updated checklist describes passage and winter visits from early September to late April. Comparisons must state the taxonomy used, because including the Yellow-billed group changes the species’ scope. Lebanese seasonality should not be generalised across Arab Africa. Seasonality and observation November falls within Lebanese winter occurrence. Distant views of flight and tail are useful, remembering that a spread tail hides its fork. A sequence during turns gives better evidence than one frame. Ecological role and conservation Carrion consumption is an ecological role, but poisons, accidental plastic ingestion and electrocution are risks. Waste, toxicant and power-line management help. Deliberately attracting kites with unknown scraps can turn apparent food into a poisoning source. articles.title: Booted Eagle
articles.body: Booted Eagle Hieraaetus pennatus Identity and identification Booted Eagle Hieraaetus pennatus belongs to Accipitridae. Pale and dark forms occur; pale birds show light body and wing coverts contrasting with dark flight feathers. Feathered legs explain the English name. Small size alone cannot separate it from buzzards. It is placed in the order Accipitriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour A mosaic of trees and open ground provides habitat. Birds, small mammals and reptiles form its prey, captured after searching from height or rapid attacks. Diet varies regionally. Tree nesting requires suitable hunting country nearby. Breeding and parental care It builds in a tree and usually lays two eggs. References give incubation around 37–40 days, principally by the female while the male supplies food, and first flight at about 50–55 days. Both contribute to care, with feeding dependence continuing after first flight. Range and Arab occurrence It breeds in parts of Europe, North Africa and western Asia, with populations migrating south. Lebanon has scarce irregular summer breeding and passage, without established regular modern winter occurrence. Older taxonomic combinations can refer to this same species. Seasonality and observation Lebanese spring passage occurs in March–April and autumn passage in August–October. November follows most usual local occurrence. Record colour form and wing and tail views without treating a dark individual as another species simply because of colour. Ecological role and conservation Loss of large trees, poison, persecution and electrical hazards are pressures. Protecting nests and woodland-open-country mosaics supports its life cycle. Exact nesting coordinates should not be publicly disclosed where this would increase disturbance or access. articles.title: Brambling
articles.body: Brambling A white-rumped winter visitor linking northern forests with the Levant and Morocco Identity and recognition The Brambling Fringilla montifringilla belongs to the finch family Fringillidae. The Lebanese guide also records the names «صليج الشمال» and «دريك الصلنج». Orange shoulders and breast, a white belly and a conspicuous white rump form its main field pattern. The breeding male has a black head and back, partly obscured by pale feather edges in winter. Females have a quieter grey-brown head and subdued orange breast. Young birds resemble the female more than the striking summer male, making wing and rump markings particularly useful. Distinguishing similar birds Bramblings often share flocks with Chaffinches. The clean white rump is their clearest distinction, supported by the orange shoulders and breast and the transition to the white belly. Chaffinches lack this white rump. Bill colour also changes: breeding males have a dark bill, whereas a yellowish bill with a dark tip is usual outside breeding. Watching a flock both in flight and on the ground reveals features that may be hidden in a single frontal photograph. Habitat, food and behaviour Breeding habitats extend across northern Eurasian woodland, including birch stands and mixed coniferous forest. In winter the species uses woodland edges, farmland and orchards with accessible seed. Beech mast is an important food in European wintering areas; other seeds and invertebrates also feature, particularly in the breeding season. Birds frequently feed on the ground and associate with other finches. Variable seed crops help explain why winter abundance can differ markedly between years. Breeding and annual cycle The cup-shaped nest occupies a tree fork, for example in birch or spruce, and incorporates grasses, moss and other plant material with a finer lining. Females normally lay five to seven eggs and perform incubation. BTO summarises typical incubation as 11–12 days and the nestling period as 13–14 days. These are breeding-cycle figures from the northern range; winter visits to Arab countries represent a different part of the annual cycle. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Arab-region occurrence is principally associated with the colder months. The Lebanese guide records regular but uncommon passage and winter presence from early October to late April in cedar, pine and fir woods and orchards. Jordan lists it as a winter visitor. Morocco’s 2017 checklist also classifies it as wintering. Kuwait’s checklist, updated in September 2026, calls it a rare winter visitor. A Levantine autumn flock therefore has a different regional context from a rare Gulf record; the scale of arrivals varies between places and years. Ecology and conservation Seed and invertebrate consumption connect this finch to woodland food webs, while migration links northern breeding forests with southern winter habitats. Its global category is Least Concern, a measure of extinction risk rather than abundance in every country. Diverse woods, orchards and winter seed supplies support visiting birds. Recording flock size, habitat and date helps distinguish a productive winter from sustained local change. Observations are best made without repeatedly flushing feeding flocks. articles.title: Brent Goose
articles.body: Brent Goose Branta bernicla A small, dark coastal goose Brent Goose Branta bernicla is a compact goose only a little larger than a Mallard, with a short black bill, black legs and a dark head, neck and breast. Adults have white patches on the sides of the neck and conspicuous white beneath the tail. The back is grey-brown, while the belly varies markedly between populations. Males and females are alike in plumage, so belly shade is not a way of identifying sex. Juveniles lack the adult neck patches at first and have a more patterned, pale-edged upperwing and back. Barnacle Goose is a useful comparison: its extensive white face differs from Brent's dark head. A distant Red-breasted Goose can also look unexpectedly dark when its chestnut colour is invisible. Check head and neck markings, body proportions and the whole plumage rather than relying on darkness alone. Brent flocks often fly in irregular lines or loose masses, accompanied by low, gruff calls. Forms and a circumpolar distribution The main familiar forms are Dark-bellied Brent, Pale-bellied Brent and Black Brant. Dark-bellied birds breed in Arctic Russia and winter mainly along western European coasts. Pale-bellied populations breed in parts of Arctic Canada, Greenland, Svalbard and Franz Josef Land, with different groups using different wintering routes. Black Brant occupy the eastern Siberian and North American Arctic sector and are closely associated with the Pacific coast outside breeding. These names describe geographic plumage groups, not seasonal changes in one bird. In Europe, Dark-bellied birds have a darker underside than Pale-bellied birds, while Black Brant typically show a strong white neck pattern and contrasting flanks. Taxonomic treatments vary in detail, so a record should describe the observed features even where a subspecies cannot be assigned confidently. North-western Europe is a principal wintering region; Arab shores lie at the margins of the usual range. Eelgrass, algae and tidal feeding Brent Geese are unusually coastal among geese. Estuaries, lagoons, shallow bays, mudflats and saltmarshes provide feeding and resting habitat. Eelgrass, marine algae including sea lettuce, and saltmarsh plants are important foods. Some populations also graze grassland or agricultural fields. Feeding may involve reaching down from the surface, tipping up in shallow water or grazing vegetation exposed by the falling tide. The availability of underwater meadows links their daily routine to water levels. California's wildlife account describes feeding particularly when eelgrass and algae become accessible at low tide, and resting in flocks on open estuarine water. It also notes that a developed salt gland permits drinking seawater. In the Arctic breeding season, terrestrial plants become more important; the Norwegian Polar Institute records scurvy-grass and mosses among foods taken in Svalbard. Breeding in the short Arctic summer Brent Geese nest on tundra, often near ponds, on islands or in low coastal terrain, as separate pairs or loose colonies. The nest is a shallow depression lined with plant material and down. In Svalbard, egg laying usually occurs in mid-June after arrival around late May or early June. These dates describe that population, not a worldwide schedule. A usual clutch contains 3–5 eggs. The female incubates, with the male nearby; BTO gives 24–26 days. Young leave the nest soon after hatching and are tended by both parents. The Norwegian Polar Institute describes fledging after about six weeks. Family groups remain together through winter into the following spring, and birds generally begin breeding at two or three years. Adults become temporarily flightless during wing moult, making undisturbed refuges particularly valuable. Morocco: documented exceptional visitors Moroccan records illustrate how far south individual Brent Geese can travel without establishing a regular wintering population. The Moroccan Rare Birds Committee's first report accepted a Dark-bellied Brent photographed at Khnifiss lagoon on 3–4 May 1994. This late-spring occurrence is a specific record, not evidence of breeding or of a predictable annual passage there. Its report for 2007 accepted a first-winter Pale-bellied bird at Salé beach on 23–30 November 2006, identifying it as Morocco's first record of that form. The report treated the species as an accidental visitor. Together these cases show both temporal and plumage diversity among rare Moroccan occurrences. The earlier committee report also cites a historical observation at Baie de l'Étoile in northern Mauritania, without assigning a subspecies. Other Arab records and their limits CMS lists Algeria and Tunisia as countries of vagrant occurrence. This places the species on their record lists, but does not establish regular coastal wintering. Egypt requires an additional historical distinction: the EORC checklist published in 2019 places Brent Goose in Category B, meaning wild records before 1950 but none thereafter accepted in that checklist. It should therefore not be presented from that evidence as a routine contemporary Egyptian winter visitor. These scattered records contrast with the large, established winter concentrations in north-western Europe. Suitable-looking estuaries around the Mediterranean do not by themselves demonstrate use by Brent Geese. At an unexpected Arab locality, photographs showing the neck, belly and upperwing can help establish both identity and age, while repeated sightings should be checked for the possibility that they concern the same individual. Conservation from sea meadows to tundra CMS and BTO give the global category as Least Concern. That does not mean all populations or sites are secure. Dependence on concentrated coastal feeding areas makes local habitat loss, recreational disturbance and changes in food supply important. The Norwegian Polar Institute links historical declines partly to loss of eelgrass on wintering grounds and intensive collection of eggs and down in the breeding range. Conservation connects both ends of the journey: tundra nesting habitat, coastal stopovers and productive winter bays. Observers should avoid flushing feeding flocks, keep dogs away and leave space at high-tide resting sites. Counts that distinguish adults from juveniles can help reveal breeding success, especially when repeated consistently across years. articles.title: Brussels to examine firearms trafficking rules and their impact on hunting and sport shooting
articles.body: The European Parliament in Brussels (archive photo). A European Parliament conference on 1 December will discuss the proposed rules and their implications for lawful activities. The European Parliament in Brussels will host a conference on 1 December 2026 to discuss the European Union’s proposal to combat illicit firearms trafficking and how to tackle crime while keeping the rules governing the lawful activities of hunters, sport shooters, manufacturers and dealers clear. Hosted by MEP Alex Agius Saliba, the event is organised with the European Federation for Hunting and Conservation (FACE) and European associations representing sporting firearms, ammunition and hunting firearms. Its title is “Navigating the EU Firearms Trafficking Proposal: Perspectives from Stakeholders”. The conference comes as lawmakers consider a draft directive presented by the European Commission on 26 February. The proposal aims to align criminal definitions and penalties for illicit firearms trafficking across EU countries, strengthen cooperation and information sharing, and help authorities trace firearms linked to crime. Why it matters for hunting and sport shooting For hunters and sport shooters, the discussion centres on drafting clear provisions that distinguish lawful activities from criminal conduct. The organisers raise the need to protect lawful users and the economic sector from legal uncertainty and disproportionate administrative burdens while strengthening the fight against trafficking. The European Commission states that its proposal targets illicit activities and does not alter the existing rules on lawful acquisition, possession or cross-border movement. The conference will give representatives of EU institutions, industry and other stakeholders an opportunity to discuss the practical effects of the proposed text on manufacturers, dealers and national authorities. The debate also covers information sharing through national firearms focal points, cooperation between countries and the digital challenges posed by blueprints used for the illicit manufacture of firearms through 3D printing. Commission, Parliament and industry perspectives According to the invitation received by Sayd Magazine, Floriana Sipala, Director for Internal Security and Counter-Terrorism Coordinator at the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Migration and Home Affairs, will deliver the keynote address. The programme includes an intervention by MEP Evin Incir, the file’s rapporteur in the Committee on Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs. MEP Malik Azmani, shadow rapporteur for the Renew Europe group, is also expected to take part, with his participation still to be confirmed in the announced programme. Industry will be represented by Olivier Van Herstraeten, Secretary General of the Association of European Manufacturers of Sporting Firearms (ESFAM), and Mauro Silvis, Secretary General of the Association of European Manufacturers of Sporting Ammunition (AFEMS) and the European Institute of Hunting and Sporting Arms (IEACS). The interventions will be followed by a question-and-answer session, with participants able to submit questions in advance when registering. A proposal still under discussion As of 11 November, the European Parliament’s legislative record shows that the file is awaiting a decision by the responsible committee. The conference therefore forms part of the ongoing legislative debate; it is not an announcement of legislation already in force or of final decisions. The in-person event will take place on Tuesday 1 December, from 17:00 to 18:30 Brussels time, in room SPINELLI 1G369 at the European Parliament. Visitors from outside Parliament must register in advance and complete the entry formalities. Photo: Oscar Franzén / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

articles.title: Caspian Tern
articles.body: Caspian Tern Hydroprogne caspia Identity and identification Caspian Tern Hydroprogne caspia belongs to Laridae; its older name is Sterna caspia. The largest tern has a massive red bill, robust body and shallowly forked tail. The breeding cap is black, becoming mixed with white outside that season. Habitat and food It searches coastal water, lakes and estuaries for fish, then dives to capture them. Open shores and islands provide resting sites. Populations differ in being resident or migratory. Breeding and development The nest is a simple ground scrape. Animal Diversity Web gives one to three eggs, shared incubation of 25–28 days and fledging around 37 days after hatching. Young still depend on feeding after flight; northern breeding dates should not be transferred to the Gulf. Arab occurrence and seasonality Qatar’s current list classifies it as a common resident breeder and winter visitor, recorded in all months. November can therefore combine resident presence with winter additions. This does not make every bird a migrant or establish nesting during that month, and Qatar’s status cannot be assigned to other Arab countries. Observation and conservation Healthy fishing areas and quiet resting and nesting sites are necessary. Distant observation avoids exposing eggs and chicks when parents are disturbed. articles.title: A chance to recover: study tracks the return of species that neared extinction
articles.body: A Lord Howe woodhen, one of the species examined in the study. Direct conservation was associated with population recovery in species reduced to fewer than 50 individuals in the wild When only a few dozen individuals of an animal species remain in the wild, saving it may seem a distant prospect. But a new study shows that direct interventions were associated with population recovery in species that had reached the brink of extinction. Researchers from Monash University and the Zoological Society of London compiled records for 147 bird and mammal species whose wild populations fell below 50 individuals at some point since 1950. Outcomes could be assessed for 141 of them. What did the numbers show? Of 51 species that received direct conservation interventions, 31 recovered to 100 individuals or more, approximately 61%. By comparison, only two of the 90 species that received no direct intervention reached that level, while 33 species in this group became extinct. Interventions included controlling invasive predators, restoring habitats, conservation breeding, translocations and releases. Six species in the group that received direct intervention also became extinct. The Lord Howe woodhen: a return spanning decades One example examined in the study is Australia’s Lord Howe woodhen. Its population fell to approximately 23 birds in the late 1970s, before measures including the removal of introduced animals, breeding and releases were implemented. By 2024, the recorded population had reached 1,638 birds. Among species that recovered after direct intervention, the median time to reach 100 individuals was approximately 18 years. The researchers note that reaching 100 individuals is a numerical benchmark for comparison, while species continue to need protection; some still depend on care and breeding outside their natural habitat. Source: study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B on 4 November 2026. Photo: Granitethighs / Wikimedia Commons. · 1 · https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/

articles.title: Cirl Bunting
articles.body: Cirl Bunting Emberiza cirlus Identity, life and distribution Cirl Bunting Emberiza cirlus is a bunting whose male has distinctive black-and-yellow facial markings. Females and young birds are less contrasting and can resemble Yellowhammers, requiring careful inspection of head and rump patterns. Its recovery in southwestern England illustrates the value of suitable farmland habitat. Collaboration between farmers and conservationists helped the population grow after severe decline, with reintroduction in Cornwall. In summer it needs invertebrates, with grasshoppers particularly important for chicks; winter food includes seeds in fields and stubbles. Thick hedges and scrub provide nesting cover, making nearby, year-round resources important. BTO reports a typical clutch of three or four eggs. This is not a rule for every population or season, and seeing a pair alone does not demonstrate successful nesting. Protecting hedges and food-rich places helps conserve its agricultural habitat. Population trends differ among regions; the British recovery alone does not describe its situation in southern Europe and North Africa. BirdLife and IUCN include Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia in its native resident range. The selected photograph comes from New Zealand, where the species was introduced; it illustrates identity, not an Arab habitat. www.bto.org — Cirl Bunting · www.rspb.org.uk — Cirl Bunting · www.rspb.org.uk — Cirl Bunting · datazone.birdlife.org — Cirl Bunting Photo: Ben Keen

articles.title: Common Moorhen
articles.body: Common Moorhen Gallinula chloropus — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and recognition The Common Moorhen, Gallinula chloropus, belongs to the rail family Rallidae, not the ducks. It is a compact waterbird about 30–38 cm long, with long greenish legs and elongated toes. Adults have a dark brown back, slaty-black underparts, a white flank line and conspicuous white beneath the tail. The bill and frontal shield are red, with a yellow bill tip. The sexes look alike; size alone is not a dependable way to sex an isolated bird. Juveniles are browner and have a dull bill, lacking the adult’s bright facial pattern. Lookalikes and behaviour The adult Eurasian Coot has a white bill and frontal shield rather than the Moorhen’s red-and-yellow bill. Moorhens frequently lift and flick the tail, exposing white markings, and can disappear rapidly into marginal vegetation. Watch both swimming birds and those walking along grassy banks. A bird hiding in reeds is not necessarily absent from a wetland census: repeated patient observations improve detection. The American Common Gallinule, Gallinula galeata, is now treated separately; older accounts that combine the two should not automatically be applied to this species. Habitat and feeding Vegetated freshwater margins are particularly important: ponds, marshes, slow waterways, reservoirs and suitable artificial wetlands all provide habitat. Reed-lined treatment-water ponds can support birds in otherwise arid landscapes. Moorhens take plant material, algae and seeds as well as aquatic and terrestrial invertebrates; small vertebrates are also eaten. They pick food from vegetation, the surface and the ground. This varied diet links land and water within the same feeding area. A pond offering both cover and accessible feeding edges differs substantially from a bare ornamental basin. Breeding and development Breeding birds defend territories, generally as pairs, though more complex mating arrangements occur. A substantial cup of stems and leaves is usually concealed in vegetation at or just above water. Both adults contribute to nesting and parental care. British nest data give typical clutches of 5–7 eggs and incubation of 20–22 days. Downy chicks leave the nest early but still receive parental care. Flight develops at approximately seven to eight weeks in British data. More than one brood can be raised, and older young sometimes help feed subsequent chicks. Arab-region occurrence and movements The species is widespread in the Old World, with resident, dispersive and migratory populations. European ringing evidence places major movements around September and March–April, with some winter recoveries in North Africa. These dates are not an exact Arabian timetable. In Saudi Arabia, artificial wetlands have enabled established breeding populations, alongside seasonal visitors. Kuwait describes local breeding residents and scarce passage and winter visitors. UAE reports document both residents and winter visitors; historical reports place winter arrivals from late August and departures through March. A year-round site may therefore contain changing individuals rather than an entirely sedentary population. Lebanon has resident breeders, with eggs recorded March–late June and immigration from mid-August to late April. Morocco likewise supports residents and winter visitors. Ecology, threats and status Moorhens consume both vegetation and small animals and themselves provide food for predators. Wetland drainage, habitat degradation and removal of shoreline cover threaten local populations. Conservation should retain vegetation while maintaining suitable water and open feeding patches. BirdLife’s 2025 global assessment lists Least Concern with a decreasing trend. Distinguish this global category from national abundance. Record juveniles, nests and dependent young separately from simple presence, and observe from a distance so a breeding record does not come at the expense of the nest. articles.title: Common Redshank: red legs beside winter wetlands
articles.body: Common Redshank Red legs and a white trailing edge to the wing identify a wader that reaches many Arab wetlands on migration and in winter. Name and classification Common Redshank, Tringa totanus, belongs to the family Scolopacidae and order Charadriiformes. Its French name is Chevalier gambette. Associated with shallow water, it is distinct from Spotted Redshank, Tringa erythropus, which can look similar outside the breeding season. Identification and age differences Adults have red or orange-red legs and a red base to the bill, with a dark tip. The upperparts are grey-brown, more strongly marked in breeding plumage; winter plumage is plainer and less patterned. In flight, a broad white trailing edge to the wing is an important feature, beyond leg colour alone. Juveniles have pale, spotted feather edges, and their legs may be less red than those of adults. The sexes look similar. Spotted Redshank has a longer, finer bill and lacks the same broad white wing edge. Identification therefore combines bill shape, wing pattern and body structure rather than a single feature. Feeding habitat and alarm behaviour It uses estuaries, saltmarshes, mudflats, lake edges and wet grasslands. It picks small invertebrates from the mud surface or probes the substrate with its bill. Coastal feeding opportunities change as mud is exposed and water recedes; safe resting places are needed when feeding grounds are flooded. It is a vocal bird and may give clear whistles when disturbed. Outside the breeding season it can occur with other waders; breeding pairs defend the area around their nests and may join in warning of danger. Breeding and life cycle It breeds across extensive parts of Eurasia, not only near the sea: waterlogged grasslands and marshes are important nesting habitats. The ground nest is concealed among vegetation, and a clutch usually contains four eggs. Chicks leave the nest and begin taking food early, but need parental protection and vegetation in which to hide. After breeding, birds move towards stopover and wintering sites; routes and distances differ between populations. Some non-breeding birds may remain in wintering areas during summer, so a summer sighting does not automatically indicate a nest. Arab distribution and seasonality Lebanese references document passage and winter occurrence, while references for Qatar and Oman describe regular passage and winter visitors. The UAE national Red List documents a non-breeding population; Iraqi and Egyptian wetland references also record the species. In North Africa it occurs among wintering wetland birds, including at Libyan sites, but the regional waterbird identification guide also reports local breeding in Tunisia and Libya. Its Arab occurrence must therefore not be described as exclusively wintering. Autumn brings renewed interest to water margins and tidal areas as migrants arrive, without implying one arrival date or equal abundance in every country. Ecological role and conservation It links mud-dwelling invertebrates to avian predators and depends on wetlands suitable for feeding, breeding and resting. Its global Least Concern (LC) classification does not rule out local or regional declines. Wet-grassland drainage, coastal alteration, pollution and disturbance are pressures worth monitoring. Protecting wintering sites must be accompanied by protection of breeding habitats along its migratory range. articles.title: Common Redstart
articles.body: Common Redstart Phoenicurus phoenicurus — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and recognition The Common Redstart, Phoenicurus phoenicurus, is a small member of the flycatcher family Muscicapidae. A breeding male combines a white forehead, black face and throat, grey back and orange-red breast and belly. Females are grey-brown above and paler below, with a warm orange wash. The rusty tail is useful in both sexes. Recently fledged young are spotted and mottled rather than miniature versions of the colourful male. Appearance also changes with season: identification should combine several features instead of relying on the breast alone. Distinguishing similar birds Females resemble female Black Redstarts, which are generally darker and more uniformly coloured; Common Redstarts tend to look warmer underneath. In males, consider the white forehead, black throat and orange underparts together. Some birds of the subspecies samamisicus have a conspicuous white wing panel, but variation and intergradation make this an insufficient subspecies test on its own. The frequently trembling tail is another helpful clue, although other redstarts share this behaviour. Habitat, food and behaviour Breeding habitat includes open woodland and old orchards where cavity-bearing trees stand above accessible feeding ground. On migration, birds also use gardens, agricultural scrub and other semi-open places. A low perch serves as a lookout: the bird drops to the ground or makes a short aerial pursuit, often returning to its perch. Insects, their larvae, spiders and other invertebrates provide food; small fruits may supplement the diet in late summer and autumn. Feeding is diurnal, whereas migration takes place mainly at night. Breeding and annual cycle A tree hole, rock crevice or wall cavity can hold the nest; suitable nestboxes are also accepted. The female constructs a cup of plant material with a finer lining. Accounts commonly give five to seven eggs and approximately two weeks of incubation by the female. Young remain dependent after leaving the nest. Breeding dates vary with latitude and habitat; local observations establish the calendar of individual Arab-region populations. BTO gives a typical incubation period of 13–14 days and fledging at about 16–17 days after hatching. Fledging precedes independence from the parents. These are general reference durations; local observations establish breeding dates in Arab countries. Arab-region distribution and seasonality This long-distance migrant winters principally in sub-Saharan Africa, including the Sahel. Jordan’s checklist identifies it as a passage migrant. The 2025 Syrian checklist describes widespread passage and limited breeding, including woodland in the northern coastal region. In Saudi Arabia, spring passage is prominent in the north and east from March to May, while autumn passage occurs especially in the west and south from September to November. Wintering is rare in the southwest, notably Tihama. An October sighting therefore fits autumn migration, but does not establish either local winter residence or breeding. Lebanon’s 2020 checklist also documents passage and scarce migrant breeding from late March to early July in open woodland and orchards, especially terraced slopes of the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges. Ecology and conservation By consuming invertebrates, redstarts participate in food webs linking vegetation and soil. Their annual cycle depends on suitable breeding, stopover and wintering habitat. Loss of old trees and cavities, intensive pesticide use, deterioration of winter quarters and drought can affect populations. The global category is Least Concern, which does not imply security everywhere and must not be confused with differing national assessments. Retaining varied orchards, cavity-bearing trees and food-rich resting places supports the bird across its annual cycle. articles.title: Common Shelduck: A Protected Waterbird and Rare Migrant in Lebanon
articles.body: Common Shelduck (Tadorna tadorna). The Common Shelduck (Tadorna tadorna) is a scarce migrant and winter visitor to Lebanon’s wetlands, coasts, and islands — a protected Anatidae species that must never be treated as game. The Common Shelduck (Tadorna tadorna; English: Common Shelduck) is known as a scarce migrant and wintering waterbird on wetlands, coasts, and islands in Lebanon. It belongs to the duck family Anatidae and is distinguished by its large size and well-balanced plumage of white, black, and chestnut-red. The male has a black head and neck with a glossy green sheen and a chestnut breast; the female is similar but with duller tones and a less prominent bill. The Common Shelduck inhabits coastal areas, saline lakes, marshes, and ponds, preferring shallow muddy or sandy waters that suit its foraging. It is widespread across Europe and Asia and migrates to the Mediterranean and North Africa in winter. Its breeding season begins in late spring and early summer. The female nests in ground burrows or rock crevices, often reusing abandoned burrows of other animals such as rabbits. She lays 8 to 12 eggs; incubation lasts 28 to 30 days. After hatching, she leads the young to water to teach them how to find food. The Common Shelduck probes mud and sand with its flattened bill. The Common Shelduck feeds on molluscs, crustaceans, worms, aquatic insects, aquatic plants, and algae, probing mud and sand with its flattened bill. It also plays an important ecological role by helping control crustacean and mollusc numbers and by improving water quality through stirring and aerating the substrate. The species faces multiple threats, chiefly habitat destruction from urban expansion and coastal development, plus environmental pollution that degrades water quality and the plants it depends on. Illegal hunting is a further threat, alongside climate change that may alter its range and feeding areas. The Common Shelduck is internationally protected under the Agreement on the Conservation of African-Eurasian Migratory Waterbirds (AEWA). It is not among the species permitted for hunting — a fact that calls for stronger protection of the bird and of its natural habitats so it can remain in the wild.

articles.title: Curlew Sandpiper
articles.body: Curlew Sandpiper Calidris ferruginea Identity and identification Curlew Sandpiper is الطيطوى النهقية in Arabic and Bécasseau cocorli in French. Calidris ferruginea belongs to Scolopacidae, order Charadriiformes. About 18–23 cm long, it combines a slender body, relatively long black legs and a long downcurved bill. Despite the reference to a curlew in its English name, it is a small sandpiper rather than one of the large curlews. Breeding adults have rusty-red underparts; winter birds are grey above and whitish below. Juveniles lack the extensive red of summer adults and show pale feather fringes. Sexes are similar, so colour alone does not establish sex. Winter Dunlin is a particular confusion species. Longer legs, a fine curved bill, upright posture and white rump help distinguish Curlew Sandpiper. Dunlin has a dark centre to the rump, whereas this bird shows a clear white patch in flight. Bill length alone is insufficient because viewing angle and individual variation affect appearances. Habitat, food and behaviour It breeds in Arctic tundra, then uses mudflats, estuaries, shallow lakes, saltpans and fresh or brackish wetlands during migration and winter. It often mixes with other sandpipers and follows falling water to newly available feeding areas. Coastal use does not exclude inland wetlands. The bill probes mud or picks surface invertebrates, including worms, molluscs, crustaceans and insect larvae. Its legs allow feeding in slightly deeper water than some smaller sandpipers, but shallow water and accessible mud remain central. Flocks also need safe resting places when the tide covers feeding ground. A site may lose value even where its mudflat survives if the roost is constantly disturbed. Breeding and development Breeding is concentrated in northern Siberia, with eggs placed in a ground scrape on tundra. The typical clutch is four; the female incubates and cares for the young. An Australian government synthesis gives 19–21 days of incubation and flight around two weeks after hatching. These are general estimates, not guaranteed intervals for every nest; other references describe information on first flight as limited. Chicks leave the nest site quickly and feed themselves while the female continues tending them. Walking and early self-feeding should be distinguished from full flight ability. Arab occurrences do not establish breeding: regional presence involves passage or wintering far from the Arctic nesting grounds. Range and Arab occurrence Non-breeding destinations extend to Africa, southern Asia and Australasia, linked by long migrations requiring a chain of stopping places. Lebanon’s 2026 guide lists a scarce passage migrant on coasts and wetlands. Oman’s official list records an abundant passage migrant and winter visitor. Arab wetlands therefore perform different functions, from a Mediterranean stopover to a winter destination on Omani shores. Local abundance does not establish global security. Kuwait’s committee list describes a common passage and summer visitor; summer presence in these waders does not establish nesting. What November means In November, a bird may be wintering or completing a movement stage, depending on population and locality. Omani observations fit established winter status; repeated presence is needed before calling a Lebanese site a regular wintering location. Record tides, numbers and accompanying species, with photographs showing shape and rump when naturally visible. Do not chase a flock simply to obtain a white-rump flight photograph. Conservation and responsible observation The current global category is Vulnerable (VU). It was uplisted from Near Threatened in the 2024 update following a global decline exceeding 30% over three generations. Threats include coastal habitat loss and reclamation, wetland degradation and disturbance, alongside local pressures such as illegal hunting. Effective protection connects feeding and resting places along migration routes rather than concentrating on one site alone. Watch from a safe margin with binoculars and leave gathering areas quiet, especially when rising water restricts the available space. articles.title: Desert Wheatear
articles.body: Desert Wheatear Oenanthe deserti Identity and identification Desert Wheatear Oenanthe deserti belongs to Muscicapidae. Males combine a black face and throat with sandy upperparts; females are duller. A mostly black tail with only a restricted white base is important, unlike the broader black-and-white patterns of other wheatears. Tail position can hide diagnostic features. It is placed in the order Passeriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Desert, gravel plains and dry open land with sparse plants provide habitat. From a stone or shrub it drops onto ground insects and other invertebrates, sometimes making short aerial sallies. Shelter and shade provide rest; desert adaptation does not mean equal activity throughout midday heat. Breeding and parental care A concealed nest occupies a cavity, space beneath a rock or suitable burrow. Invertebrates feed growing nestlings, and care continues after nest departure. Food and seasonal conditions influence breeding in arid habitats; European or Asian calendars should not be imposed on every Arab desert. Range and Arab occurrence Its North African and Asian range includes Arab deserts, with both resident and migratory populations. Lebanon’s checklist describes scarce irregular autumn passage and rare spring passage, rather than widespread residence. Parts of Arabia receive wintering birds. Seasonality and observation November suits observation in desert wintering areas, while following most usual Lebanese autumn passage. Views of spread tail, face and wings improve identification. Location and date matter because age and sex reduce the value of colour alone. Ecological role and conservation It consumes invertebrates and feeds desert raptors. Loss of scattered vegetation, land levelling and off-road driving are pressures. Retaining rocks and plant patches preserves food, shade and nesting places in terrain that may look empty but supports varied life. articles.title: Dunlin: a small wader linking the north to Arab shores
articles.body: Dunlin Its plumage changes from a black summer belly to winter grey, while its journeys connect northern breeding habitats with passage and wintering coasts. Name and classification Dunlin, Calidris alpina, is a small wader in the family Scolopacidae and order Charadriiformes. Its French name is Bécasseau variable. Arabic references use both al-durayja al-albiyya and al-durayja al-mutaghayyira; these alternative names do not denote different species. Plumage, age and similar species It has a black bill curving slightly downwards and dark legs. Breeding plumage includes a black belly patch and reddish-brown patterned upperparts; in winter, the back is grey and the belly white. Birds arriving in autumn may retain some summer feathers, so individuals need not look identical. Juveniles show stronger patterning and pale edges to their back feathers, with dark spotting below. The sexes look similar and bill length varies, so a general photograph does not establish sex. Curlew Sandpiper, Calidris ferruginea, usually has longer legs and a longer bill; Sanderling, Calidris alba, is paler in winter and shorter-billed. These features must be considered together because age and moult complicate comparisons. Food and the tidal rhythm It takes worms, molluscs, crustaceans, insects and other invertebrates by picking or probing wet mud and sand. Coastal feeding areas change with the tides; when water covers the mudflats, birds gather at nearby roosts. Its close-knit flocks are striking: as they turn, they appear alternately dark and pale. Small groups also occur beside inland lakes and pools during passage. Large numbers at one site do not establish that the species is secure throughout its range. Life cycle and breeding Breeding areas lie mainly in northern, Arctic and sub-Arctic regions, including tundra, grasslands and wet peatlands. The nest is on the ground and a clutch usually contains four eggs. Chicks can move and seek food early but still need care and protection while growing. After breeding, populations leave for wintering areas along different routes. Ringing data show that some European breeders reach North Africa, whereas other populations travel elsewhere. Dunlins in Arab countries do not all originate in one country or follow a single route. Arab distribution and seasonal relevance Its Arab range extends from Mauritania and the Maghreb to Egypt, the Levant, Iraq, the Gulf and the Arabian Peninsula, with local differences in abundance and occurrence. Banc d’Arguin in Mauritania is particularly important as a wintering area for some northern populations. Libyan winter surveys document coastal distribution and use of some inland wetlands. In Lebanon it is recorded as a passage migrant and winter visitor; in Oman it is a regular wader during passage and winter. Autumn is therefore a useful season to look along coasts and pools. An out-of-season bird does not by itself establish residence or breeding, and inclusion on a national list does not mean regular numbers occur at every site in that country. Ecology and conservation The IUCN global assessment of 2024 classified Dunlin as Near Threatened (NT), with an overall declining trend. This supersedes references still displaying its former Least Concern category. Its future depends on northern breeding habitats and on passage and wintering sites together. Loss of mudflats, wetland degradation and disturbance affect opportunities to feed and rest. Observers can help by recording species, location and date while avoiding intrusion into roosts or repeatedly forcing birds to fly.
