articles.title: European Greenfinch
articles.body: European Greenfinch Chloris chloris — A seed-eater of orchards, woodland edges and gardens Name and identity The European Greenfinch, also called al-khudayri in the Lebanese guide, is Chloris chloris, a member of Fringillidae within Passeriformes. Older references may call it Carduelis chloris: these are taxonomic names for the same species. AviList 2026 uses Chloris. Its native range spans much of Europe, North Africa and western Asia; introduced populations also occur elsewhere. “European” in its English name does not exclude native breeding populations in Arab countries. Identification A stocky body, heavy conical bill and short, slightly forked tail are characteristic. Males are olive-green with conspicuous yellow on the wings and tail sides; females are greyer and browner but retain diagnostic yellow areas. Juveniles resemble females with stronger streaking. European Goldfinch differs in its red face and black-and-white head; Siskin is smaller, slimmer and more streaked, with a finer bill. Greenness alone is unreliable for sexing or ageing because light and feather wear alter its appearance. Bill shape, yellow markings and overall build should be considered together. Habitat, food and behaviour It uses orchards, gardens, open woodland, forest edges and farmland interspersed with trees and shrubs. Plant food, especially grass, tree and shrub seeds, dominates its diet. Its strong bill handles harder seeds than those accessible to many fine-billed birds. It moves between the ground, branches and seed-bearing plants, forming non-breeding flocks that may mix with other finches. The male sings from an exposed perch, combining repeated phrases with prolonged wheezing notes. Its presence around people reflects food and cover, rather than a universal need for artificial feeding. Breeding and parental care The female builds a cup nest in a tree or shrub, using plant material with a finer lining. BTO gives a typical clutch of four or five eggs and female incubation of about 14 days; the male feeds her during this period. Chicks receive regurgitated food including seeds, initially from the female and later also from the male. They leave the nest at approximately 14–16 days, with parental feeding continuing as flight and foraging skills develop. More than one brood can be raised. These are reference durations; the 2026 Lebanese guide places local breeding between mid-March and mid-August, varying with site, altitude and conditions. Distribution and migration in the Arab region Native populations occur in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and the Levant, with the range extending to northern Iraq. AviList also records northeastern Egypt and winter movements of Levantine populations towards Sinai and Egypt. In Lebanon it is a very common resident breeder and winterer, with smaller passage movements in spring and autumn. A November observation therefore need not represent a newly arrived migrant. In contrast, Kuwait’s checklist treats it as a vagrant. Partial migration differs among populations: some northern birds move south, while others remain resident or make local movements. Ecological role and conservation AviList 2026 conservation data classify it globally as Least Concern. Disease, habitat loss, hunting and trapping can nevertheless affect local populations. British studies linked a major decline to trichomonosis; that geographical evidence is not a diagnosis of Lebanese birds. Avoid concentrating birds at dirty or crowded feeding points, and retain fruiting trees, shrubs and seed-rich field margins. The species illustrates the wildlife value of botanically varied gardens and orchards. Repeated counts at consistent sites are more informative about local change than a single casual sighting. articles.title: European Stonechat
articles.body: European Stonechat Saxicola rubicola — Identification, habitats, breeding and seasonal occurrence in the Arab region Identity and recognition The European Stonechat, Saxicola rubicola, is a small member of the flycatcher family Muscicapidae. Older publications sometimes treated stonechats within a broader species; modern taxonomy separates European, Siberian and African stonechats, each with its own distribution. A male has a very dark, often black-looking head, white neck-side patches, an orange-red breast and a mottled brown back. Females are duller, with a brown head and back and an orange-tinged breast. Feather condition and lighting also alter a male’s apparent contrast. Age and similar species Juveniles are mottled. Adult age cannot generally be established precisely from appearance alone, and moult and feather wear change visible patterns. Sex or age should not be assigned from a distant, unclear photograph. The Siberian Stonechat, Saxicola maurus, can be similar: no single white patch is sufficient for identification. Plumage features, locality, season and reliable photographic provenance should be considered together. Whinchats usually show a conspicuous pale eyebrow. Clear observations of several features are more useful than a first impression of colour. Habitat, food and behaviour European Stonechats use open country with grasses, low scrub, agricultural margins and slightly elevated lookout perches. A bird often watches from a shrub top or plant stem before dropping to seize a small prey item. Insects and other invertebrates dominate the diet, supplemented by fruit or seeds. Exposed perching and wing movements make the species noticeable; its short calls suggest two stones striking together, explaining the English name. A mixture of low vegetation and open space suits this bird. Breeding and life cycle The nest is low or on the ground, hidden in dense vegetation. British records typically show five or six eggs and two or three broods, with female incubation around fourteen days and young leaving after roughly 14–15 days. These are British reference observations; dates and brood numbers vary among populations. Breeding in the bird’s area of origin must also be distinguished from winter occurrence in the Levant: a bird wintering in a Lebanese field may nest elsewhere. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Lebanon’s 2020 checklist describes a common passage migrant and winter visitor from mid-September to late April, using open mountain habitats and Aammiq. Jordan’s list records passage and winter presence, whereas Oman’s official list, version 8.0 of 1 January 2026, describes an uncommon passage migrant and winter visitor. Some European populations move south towards North Africa; residency and migration vary among populations. Late October falls within the period of arrival and winter residence in the Levant, where birds use grassland and low scrub. Ecology and conservation By consuming invertebrates and serving as prey, the Stonechat belongs to open-country food webs. Its global category is Least Concern in the scientific reference used here, not a separate assessment of every Arab locality. Removal of rough grass and scrub and fragmentation of suitable habitat can reduce feeding and nesting opportunities; severe winters have affected European populations. Retaining grassy margins and scattered shrubs preserves its habitat structure without converting open land into dense woodland. articles.title: European warning: 11–36 million birds illegally killed or captured annually in the Mediterranean
articles.body: Illegal bird nets in Lebanon’s Bekaa, 1 October 2026 — Sayd archive / Adonis Elkhateeb, Editor-in-Chief. An estimated 11 to 36 million birds are illegally killed or captured annually across the Mediterranean, according to a 2016 scientific study whose findings were highlighted again by conservation organisations on 10 October 2026. This figure featured in a warning issued by Tour du Valat, EuroNatur and BirdLife International on 10 October 2026, World Migratory Bird Day, calling for more effective protection along migration routes. According to the warning, 83% of the 46 assessed countries have yet to take sufficient measures to meet the commitment to halve illegal killing and capture by 2030. The organisations called for closing legal gaps, strengthening field monitoring and awareness, and wider cooperation between public authorities, hunters and conservation groups. Lebanon on the migration route In Lebanon's Bekaa Valley, Sayd Magazine's archive documents the removal of nets used for trapping birds, an example of the risks migratory species face along the route. Countering indiscriminate trapping is compatible with safeguarding responsible and lawful hunting within applicable seasons and regulations. An international project for the Egyptian vulture Egyptian vulture — Charles J. Sharp / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0). Also on 10 October, the Bulgarian Society for the Protection of Birds announced the LIFE EV Safe Return project, bringing together 15 organisations and institutions from Europe, the Middle East and Africa. Running until 2031, it aims to improve the prospects of the Egyptian vulture, a migratory raptor travelling over 5,000 kilometres between the Balkans and its wintering areas in Africa. The project addresses poison baits, illegal hunting and electrocution on unsafe power infrastructure. Both initiatives highlight the need for coordinated cross-border protection, from nesting areas to stopover sites and wintering grounds.

articles.title: Ferruginous Duck
articles.body: Ferruginous Duck Aythya nyroca — A Near Threatened chestnut duck linking Arab breeding wetlands with winter lakes Identity and recognition The Ferruginous Duck, Aythya nyroca, is a diving duck in the family Anatidae. The male combines rich chestnut plumage, a darker back and a very pale, almost white iris. Its crown is slightly peaked and its bill dark grey. White undertail-coverts and a broad white wing stripe in flight are important recognition features. At approximately 38–42 cm long, it is smaller and less bulky than some accompanying diving ducks. Age, sex and similar species Females share the general pattern but are duller and have brown eyes. Juveniles resemble females, with duller brown plumage and less clean white on the belly and undertail. A dark eye therefore does not rule out the species. The male Common Pochard has a grey body and black breast, while Tufted Ducks possess a conspicuous crest. Female diving ducks and some hybrids can complicate identification: head and bill shape, eye colour, undertail and wing pattern should be considered together rather than as interchangeable single clues. Habitats, diet and behaviour Shallow freshwater rich in submerged and floating plants, with reedbeds or dense marginal cover, is favoured habitat. Some brackish pools are also used. It feeds by diving and taking food near the surface, consuming seeds, roots and other aquatic plant material alongside invertebrates. Its tendency to remain near vegetation can make it difficult to detect even on a large lake. Outside breeding it may associate with other diving ducks. Open-water gaps among plants supply feeding, swimming and resting space; the combination of cover and accessible water is important. Breeding and life cycle Nests occur close to water in dense vegetation, on plant platforms or on floating islets. Biological references give a usual clutch of 7–10 eggs, incubation of approximately 25–28 days and flight at around 55–60 days. Research published in 2021 examined fifty nests at Algeria’s Lake Tonga during 2016 and 2017, linking breeding outcomes to nest-site characteristics and nest density. Some females deposited eggs in other nests of their own species, helping explain exceptionally large egg totals. The lake is consequently a breeding habitat, not merely a winter refuge. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Its Arab distribution includes different seasonal roles. It breeds at Algerian wetlands including Tonga, while BirdLife identifies Egypt’s Lake Nasser as an important wintering area. Lebanon’s 2020 checklist records scarce September–March passage and winter birds, with occasional non-breeding summer visitors. In Iraq, a study published in 2011 documented nests and families at Dalmaj marshes during May 2010. Autumn therefore connects regional breeding populations with arrivals from farther away, while a summer sighting alone need not indicate an active nest. Ecology and conservation The global category is Near Threatened, reaffirmed by BirdLife in an August 2026 publication. Pressures include wetland loss, vegetation degradation, altered water conditions, drought and excessive hunting. Survival depends on connected breeding, stopover and wintering sites rather than protection of one lake alone. Suitable water regimes, varied vegetation and quiet areas support feeding and nesting. Watching from a distance avoids forcing birds into flight for photographs, particularly at small sites where disturbance can repeatedly interrupt their activities. articles.title: Field balance: Beretta A400 Xtreme Plus or Benelli SBE 3? Gas versus inertia
articles.body: Beretta A400 Xtreme Plus in the field: an empty hull ejects on the shot. Editorial photo. Ask a hunter at first light on the firing line what shotgun they swear by, and the debate may never end. Narrow it to Italy’s two leading semi-auto schools, and the contest usually returns to the same pair: the Beretta A400 Xtreme Plus and the Benelli Super Black Eagle 3 (SBE 3). Both guns — most often in 12-gauge with a 3½-inch (89 mm) chamber — are mature designs with long field pedigrees. The real difference does not show on climate-controlled shelves; it shows in wadis, on coastal sand, and in cold spray. Gas breath versus inertia Beretta A400 Xtreme Plus. Manufacturer-style photo (Beretta). Beretta A400 (Blink) gas system: Powder gas drives the bolt back, ejects the hull, and chambers the next round. With Kick-Off in the stock, felt recoil is typically softer. On fast flocks — rock dove or turtle dove — that helps keep the muzzle on the line for a second and third shot, and shoulders notice it after a long day. Benelli Super Black Eagle 3 (SBE 3). Manufacturer-style photo (Benelli USA). Benelli SBE 3 (Inertia Driven): No gas pistons and far less carbon packing in gas tubes. A spring in the bolt group uses recoil motion to cycle the action. The forend is slimmer, the gun is often lighter, and pointability on snap shots is a clear strength. Reliability in dirt is the other headline: light mud or sand can often be brushed off so you are back shooting without a full strip-down — a trait coastal and marsh hunters value. Which way does the scale tip? If your days are long on foot and you want a lighter gun with simpler cleanup, many hunters lean to the Benelli SBE 3. If you sit fixed blinds, shoot heavier loads, and want clearer recoil absorption with a quicker second and third bird, the Beretta A400 Xtreme Plus makes a strong field case. There is no absolute winner — only the system that matches your ground, your shoulder, and how you hunt.

articles.title: “From the Poem to the Maqnas”: A Migration Journey in Arab Memory
articles.body: Each autumn, as the air shifts and birds begin their passage over the region’s skies, an old feeling comes back. The maqnas—the traditional hunt outing, with its waiting and its quiet—is more than a day in the open country. It is a cultural word that has long lived in language and in image. Let us follow the bird on a reverse migration, from our present into heritage. In classical Arabic literature, hunting scenes were never idle decoration; they tested a poet’s power of sight. Those images took shape in the Abbasid age in what are known as tardiyyat—Abbasid hunting poems. One opening by Abu Nuwas is enough to show how he saw the scene: he sets out before the clear brightness of morning, before the dark hens begin to cluck, while night is still wrapped in its own hide—pitch-black, as if its dye had not yet been stripped away. Here the hunt is not cast as an act but as a pure visual moment: night withdrawing, the horse rising. Abu Nuwas then turns to the tools of the chase—the horse that carries him, and a hound whose household lives by the animal’s labor, whose deep-set jaws and long cheek mean gazelles meet only hardship in the drive. Beside falcon and hound, the Arabs also hunted with cheetahs—a practice that left its mark in descriptions of the leap and the strike. Today a magazine reader may never go out into the open country, and may settle for an image on a screen or a poem in an old book. Even so, the feeling stays near: a yearly rhythm that binds Arab memory to the paths of birds over desert and plain. Classical poetry did not invent that feeling; it gave it a high language, and so it became a store we return to whenever the sky begins to move. In that sense, maqnas grows wider than the outing itself. It may mean a family inheritance told at leisure, a literary image learned at school, or the distance that opens between “season news” and “reading heritage.” Contemporary readers bring scientific pictures of migration routes, and that gives the old text a second life. The poem that described the hawk or the horse celebrated precision and attention—the qualities that give a relationship with nature its depth. Arab hunting verse was not always a cry in the wild; often it was directed silence: waiting, watching, a slow account of detail. Autumn, with its migrants, gives that silence a natural stage—flocks passing, colors shifting, distances that remind us wildlife is larger than the moment of capture. From poem to maqnas, from the tardiyya to the sense of migrants in the sky, one cultural thread runs on. In the Arab imagination the hunt was always larger than a passing act; it was a way of looking, a rhythm, and one of literature’s frontiers in facing the world. When the flocks pass overhead, that old rhythm still sounds in memory—like a journey that never quite ends.

articles.title: Gadwall
articles.body: Gadwall Mareca strepera — a dabbling duck with a white wing patch Identity and name The Gadwall, called “al-batt al-sumari” and “sumariya” in Arabic references, belongs to Anatidae and the order Anseriformes. The scientific name used here is Mareca strepera; older references and some regional checklists use Anas strepera for the same species. It is a dabbling duck rather than a diving duck that normally feeds completely underwater. A male may look dull from a distance, but binoculars reveal intricate patterning rather than uniform grey. Identification A male in characteristic plumage is grey-brown, finely patterned across the body, with a black rear end and a dark bill. The wing has a white patch, with black and chestnut areas visible on closer inspection. The forehead is steep and the body a little slimmer than a Mallard’s. The female is mottled brown, with orange edges to her dark bill; the white wing patch shows in flight and may be visible at rest. Juveniles resemble females, so the absence of grey does not determine sex or age. Males also acquire female-like eclipse plumage after breeding. The white wing patch, narrower bill and pale belly help distinguish Gadwall from Mallard; these features should be assessed together rather than relying on one colour or a distant photograph. Habitat and food Gadwall use lakes, ponds and marshes rich in aquatic vegetation, in fresh and sometimes brackish water, both natural and artificial. They usually feed near the surface, tipping forwards to reach submerged plants. Leaves, stems and seeds are important foods; invertebrates, including insects and small molluscs, become more important during breeding. They may take vegetation gathered by other birds, including coots and diving ducks, as these return to the surface. Behaviour and life cycle They mix with other ducks and form flocks outside the breeding season; pairs may already be evident in autumn and winter. The female builds a ground nest concealed by vegetation and lined with plant material and down; small islands sometimes provide suitable sites. BTO records give a typical clutch of 9–11 eggs, incubated by the female for about 24–26 days. Chicks hatch covered in down and able to move, and usually become capable of flight at around 45–50 days. These are reference durations, not a uniform calendar for every population. Distribution and migration The breeding range extends across large parts of North America, Europe and Asia, with local breeding in northwestern Africa. Northern populations are strongly migratory, whereas others remain resident or move shorter distances. In Europe, birds undergo a post-breeding wing moult that temporarily prevents flight before continuing their movements. Summer presence alone therefore does not demonstrate permanent residency or nesting at a site. Occurrence in Arab countries The North African waterbird guide documents winter occurrence in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt and Sudan, without extending that generalisation to Mauritania. This describes distribution, not equal abundance in every country or wetland. Lebanon’s 2020 checklist describes a very scarce, irregular winter visitor from late October to mid-March. In Kuwait it is an uncommon passage migrant and scarce winter visitor, and breeding has been recorded; nesting cannot therefore be ruled out across the entire region. Oman lists it as a fairly common winter visitor. The UAE checklist describes an uncommon to fairly common migrant and winter visitor, but seldom numerous. Records from Dhahran, Saudi Arabia, describe an uncommon winter visitor during October–March; this is local evidence, not a classification for the whole kingdom. Why late October? This period overlaps part of the species’ autumn movements; in Lebanon, the documented winter occurrence window begins late in the month. It is not a single peak throughout the Arab world and does not guarantee birds at every lake. Recording dates, counts and water conditions is useful; watch quietly without making birds stop feeding or abandon their resting place. Conservation and pressures The 2025 global Red List assessment classifies Gadwall as Least Concern (LC). This does not mean local problems are absent: the assessment identifies water pollution, disturbance from recreation, hunting across much of the range, and lead poisoning through ingestion in Spain. Protecting vegetation and feeding, nesting and resting sites supports the species; global abundance does not replace country-level monitoring. articles.title: George Scott expands in Dubai with 19 horses and a permanent Meydan base
articles.body: An illustrative archive photograph of horse racing. The British trainer is preparing for the 2026–27 Carnival from Grandstand Stables following earlier success in the UAE. British trainer George Scott is preparing for the 2026–27 Dubai Racing Carnival with a 19-horse team operating from a new base at Meydan Racecourse, expanding his Middle Eastern presence after successful seasons in the region. Scott’s team will be based at Grandstand Stables at Meydan, where he is establishing his first permanent Dubai base. The project is backed by a group of owners led by Victorious Forever, alongside prominent names from the UAE and international racing. The 38-year-old said his results on previous Middle Eastern campaigns had encouraged a more settled presence in Dubai, describing the new base as an important step in his team’s development. Success that paved the way Scott has recorded four wins from 28 starts in the UAE. His Dubai Carnival success began in 2019, when Another Batt won as the trainer’s very first Carnival runner. In 2025, West Acre strengthened that record by winning the Group 2 Blue Point Sprint and the Group 3 Nad Al Sheba Sprint. Force And Valour, owned by Victorious Forever, also won on dirt last season and returns for a third Carnival. New horses and Dubai owners Scott’s new squad includes Group 3-placed Saber Strike and the Resolute Racing-owned Rogue Legend, who has joined him from US trainer Wesley Ward. Shiplake will represent Dubai Racing Club Chairman Sheikh Rashed Dalmook Al Maktoum, while Zoar and Mr Colonel race for his brother Sheikh Hamdan Dalmook Al Maktoum. Michael Blencowe, the owner of West Acre, is represented by Listed winner Command The Stars and Lil Koulsty, both owned in partnership. Victorious Forever has also purchased Wiki, a Listed winner in France, to join the team. Its colours will also be carried by Varzi, Gamri, Instant Force, Rizal, Wave Rider, Commander’s Intent and Major Neigh Sayer. El Matador, He’s A Monster and Zubaru complete the team. A long-term Middle Eastern presence Scott believes the new base will offer owners greater access to major international racing opportunities while maintaining the standards of horse care and attention to detail followed at his British yard, Eve Lodge. He said the ambition was to build on earlier international results with the strength of the new team and the backing of its owners. Establishing a base in a new environment will require continued learning and adaptation as the project develops. He hopes the move will mark the beginning of a long and successful Middle Eastern presence for his team. Dubai Racing Club announced plans in September for a Scott base with capacity for 20 horses. The new release adds the details of the squad preparing for the season, within a plan that allows the horses to compete at Meydan and other UAE racecourses, including Abu Dhabi, Sharjah and Jebel Ali. articles.title: George Taza: We Must All Take Part in Protecting Fish Stocks
articles.body: George Taza, head of the Lebanese Fishermen page. An interview with George Taza, head of the “Lebanese Fishermen” page — on illegal methods at sea, weak enforcement, women anglers, and a shared duty to protect fish stocks. The sea has its own world! Underwater we enjoy watching marine creatures, coral, and caves; on the surface we enjoy the calm of the horizon, relax under the sun, converse with moonlight, and dance to the sound of the waves… That is how George Taza — head of the “Lebanese Fishermen / الصياد اللبناني” page — sees it. From the conversation: I began this hobby on my first outing with my father in 1999. Hunters face many problems, including illegal, abusive fishing — putting poison in bread and throwing it to catch fish, blasting, or dredging — all violations with severe consequences for fish stocks. Disrespect for marine fishing laws stems from lack of accountability, absence of monitoring, and scarce awareness programmes from the relevant ministry. The state as a whole has a duty to monitor and to stop dumping waste into the sea, because it is a livelihood for many fishermen. Fishing is both a hobby and a livelihood, always in need of development. Every fisherman’s experience helps raise the level of the craft. “The sea is treacherous” — but in our lexicon it means fishing and passion; that does not cancel the need for caution and safety. The landfill project over the seal cave in Amchit was stopped by a decision of the Ministry of Environment after complaints from environmental activists and after our rapid mobilisation and posting of photos on social media. Young women compete with men in sea fishing; they have patience and composure. Often, when you reel in the line, a large fish comes to seize the one already hooked and pulls the line loaded with hooks; a fish fighting for its life can also injure you — these are among fishing’s risks. We laugh a lot when a fish slips off the hook inside the boat between our feet — and when fish leap at night as the boat moves and land aboard. The sea’s bounty is great; we must all take part in protecting fish stocks and respecting the law. What is needed: awareness in schools; monitoring fish markets; media awareness programmes; more visits to ports; and follow-up on fishermen’s problems so they become partners in conserving fish stocks.

articles.title: Greater Short-toed Lark
articles.body: Greater Short-toed Lark Calandrella brachydactyla A small bird whose name needs care The Greater Short-toed Lark, Calandrella brachydactyla, is a small bird linking Mediterranean plains and Arabian deserts with wintering grounds farther south. It measures about 14–15 centimetres. “Greater” is a relative term distinguishing it from other short-toed larks: it is not large compared with a Calandra Lark or Skylark. It belongs to the lark family and spends much of the day on the ground, where its sandy-brown upperparts are difficult to separate from stones and soil. The scientific name must be understood in its modern sense. Older publications sometimes used broader species concepts that included eastern populations subsequently separated as other species. Not every historical map labelled “short-toed lark” can therefore be transferred automatically to this bird. Nor does its name mean an observer must catch it or photograph its toes. Field identification relies on the combination of shape, plumage and voice. Identification and similar species This is a small lark with pale underparts, a short conical bill and a pale eyebrow. The adult breast is less heavily streaked than in many similar larks, with two small dark patches near its sides that vary in prominence. The streaked head and back blend with sparsely vegetated open ground, especially when the bird crouches and hides its breast from view. One patch, which the viewing angle may conceal, is not enough to establish identity. Comparison with short-toed larks of the genus Alaudala requires care. Those birds tend to have more streaked breasts and differences in build and bill, but changes with age and feather condition limit the usefulness of any single feature. Similar small eastern larks add to the difficulty in some passage areas. The length of feathers on the closed wing, head shape, calls and photographs from several angles all help. It is unsafe to assume that every member of a mixed flock belongs to the same species. Males and females look broadly similar. Young birds appear more spotted or scalloped because of pale feather edges. These differences do not always permit accurate sexing or ageing at a distance. Some older guides also use “Lesser Short-toed Lark” in a broad taxonomic sense. A modern photograph should not be compared with an old name without checking which species was intended, particularly when documenting an unusual record. Sparse vegetation and changing food The bird uses dry steppe, fallow land, lightly vegetated fields and open sandy or gravelly surfaces. It favours space to walk and reach food between plants rather than continuous tall grass. Kuwaiti references describe it on desert ground, dried mudflats and irrigated fields with short, scattered vegetation. Its use of some irrigated farmland does not mean that converting all steppe to intensive agriculture would improve its habitat. It collects seeds and invertebrates while walking on the ground. Insects become more important during breeding, whereas seeds predominate outside that period. A seemingly suitable field can change when margins are removed, soil is turned or pesticides are applied. Birds present after harvest may be exploiting a seasonal resource, not completing every stage of their life cycle in that field. Feeding and resting can occur at one site while nesting or roosting takes place elsewhere. Autumn and winter movements The breeding range extends across parts of northwestern Africa, southern Europe and western and central Asia. Migratory populations travel towards the African Sahel, the Arabian Peninsula and farther towards southern Asia. Migration is especially pronounced in some northern populations, while movements of southern populations differ. Modern taxonomy makes it particularly important not to extend the range eastwards using old maps produced before very similar species were separated. Birds travel in flocks that can include other small species, and migration occurs both by day and at night. Seeing a flock in November does not establish that it is still heading south: it may already have reached its wintering area. Repeated visits can distinguish a brief stop from longer occupation, provided the observer does not assume that birds seen on two visits are the same individuals. Flock size, date and location are more useful than an undefined claim of “heavy occurrence”. Pairing and nest construction The male sings in an aerial display over suitable ground, and birds form breeding pairs. The season starts in spring across many parts of the range, but timing depends on location and conditions. Spanish references describe a local spring-to-summer calendar, which should not be generalised to Arabia, where plant and invertebrate productivity also responds to rainfall. Summer presence in a country does not prove that every bird is breeding, since residents and passage birds may overlap. The female makes a small hollow or uses an existing one and builds a cup of grasses, roots and softer material, usually sheltered by a short plant. Soil particles and pebbles may reinforce the exposed side. The Saudi reference assigns nest construction and incubation to the female, with both parents feeding the young. This nest is protected by concealment rather than height, making trampling, cultivation and off-road driving dangerous even on apparently empty ground. Eggs and the growth of chicks The Saudi account describes three to five eggs and incubation lasting about 11–13 days. Chicks leave the nest at around nine to ten days, then hide nearby before flying at approximately 12–15 days. Some European references extend the clutch range to six eggs. These are different reference ranges, not a rule requiring every nest to contain one fixed number. Two broods can occur in a season when conditions allow, and parental care remains important after the young leave the nest. Nest departure, flight and independence are three different stages. A healthy youngster should not be removed from the ground merely because its nest is no longer visible: its parents may be close. If an adult carrying food hesitates to approach, withdrawing quietly is better than following it to discover where the chicks are hidden. Different seasonal roles in Arab countries Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia form part of the North African breeding range, while migrants also pass through parts of the region. Mauritania, Sudan and Somalia lie within the broader African wintering range, with numbers and sites varying between years. This helps explain November observations: declining numbers on a northern breeding ground can coincide with arrival in Arab lands farther south, rather than indicating permanent local disappearance. The Middle Eastern range includes populations associated with Sinai, the Levant and Iraq, and is not confined to a coastal migration corridor. Saudi references make a clear distinction: a very common passage migrant, common winter visitor and rare breeding migrant in small numbers. Breeding takes place on irrigated or cultivated land with scattered cover, while winter habitat extends into desert plains. Old estimates of breeding pairs should not be presented as the results of a current census. Kuwaiti references document abundant passage, summer and winter visits, and breeding. In Oman, the regional review describes common passage and winter occurrence, with scattered breeding reports that should be distinguished from the better-established winter status. These roles are more varied than a brief transit alone. An individual cannot be assigned to a subspecies or country of origin merely because a flock arrives in a familiar season; establishing origin requires tracking or other independent evidence. Conservation and the value of open land AviList 2026 records the species as globally Least Concern, LC. Nevertheless, loss of fallow land, agricultural intensification and removal of low vegetation can reduce habitat and food. Protection requires maintaining breeding, stopover and wintering sites together: success in one does not automatically compensate for loss of another. A large flock can indicate birds concentrated around a limited resource rather than abundant habitat across the landscape. Observe from a field edge or existing track without blocking the flock's direction of movement or repeatedly forcing it to take flight. Avoid playback to attract breeding males and do not publicise nest locations. Record unresolved similar-looking birds separately instead of including them in a confirmed species total. Finally, hunting laws remain independent of global conservation status: a Least Concern category does not determine whether hunting is legal in any particular country. articles.title: Greater White-fronted Goose
articles.body: Greater White-fronted Goose Anser albifrons Identity and identification Greater White-fronted Goose Anser albifrons belongs to Anatidae. Adults show white around the bill base, irregular black belly bars and orange legs. Young birds lack some of these marks; head, bill and body proportions help separate the species from Lesser White-fronted Goose. Habitat and food It grazes in open, damp landscapes and rests on quiet water. Flocks commute between feeding and roosting areas, so conservation must retain both. Breeding and development It breeds in northern regions in a lined ground nest. BTO gives a typical clutch of 5–6 eggs, incubated by the female for 27–28 days. Downy young walk early; the reference fledging age is 40–43 days. Walking ability does not imply flight. Arab occurrence and seasonality Lebanon’s 2020 checklist documents passage and irregular winter occurrence, usually from mid-November to early March. Qatar’s current list describes a rare winter visitor. November precedes the main Lebanese winter period; presence in Qatar remains rare. Neither status describes a resident population. Observation and conservation Chasing flocks and draining wetlands reduce feeding and resting opportunities. Avoid approaching roosts to force birds into flight for photographs. articles.title: Grey Plover
articles.body: Grey Plover Pluvialis squatarola — An Arctic breeder linked to Arab tidal shores Identity and identification Grey Plover is a member of Charadriidae, retained as Pluvialis squatarola in AviList 2026. Its relatively bulky body, large head, stout black bill and dark legs help establish its identity. Winter birds are mottled grey above and predominantly pale below. The alternative English name Black-bellied Plover describes breeding plumage rather than the appearance most observers encounter on Arab shores in November. Age, sex and similar species Breeding plumage includes a black face, breast and belly bordered by white; females generally show less uninterrupted black than males. Individual variation and changing plumage make sexing a distant bird unreliable. Juveniles have yellowish spotting above. Black axillary feathers, visible beneath an open wing, are the decisive feature separating this species from golden plovers in every plumage. Wait for a natural stretch or flight rather than flushing a bird to obtain this diagnostic view. A single grey-looking photograph may not securely establish either age or sex. Habitats, food and behaviour Outside the breeding season it uses sandy beaches, tidal mudflats, estuaries and coastal lagoons, occasionally visiting inland waters. It searches visually, advancing and pausing before taking prey from the surface or shallow substrate. Marine worms, crustaceans, molluscs and other invertebrates are important foods. Feeding space changes with the tide, while safe high-tide resting places allow birds to conserve energy when exposed flats disappear. A resting flock is therefore using an essential part of its habitat, not merely occupying an empty beach. Breeding and life cycle Breeding takes place on Arctic tundra, not on the Arab coasts used in winter. A shallow ground nest normally contains four eggs. Both parents contribute to care; chicks leave the nest after hatching and find food under parental protection. Migration connects these northern breeding grounds with a sequence of staging areas and temperate or tropical coasts. Individuals and age classes do not all travel at once, so arrivals and departures overlap rather than obeying a single universal date. Distribution and seasonality in the Arab world In the Arab world this is primarily a coastal passage migrant and winter visitor, using North African, Red Sea, Gulf and Arabian Sea shores. Aden waterbird accounts document passage and winter occurrence, while Emirati environmental sources describe autumn migration. Lebanese scientific checklists treat it as an uncommon passage and winter bird of the coast and islands, not a resident breeder. November finds many birds on wintering grounds, although movements continue according to locality, weather and tides. Summer presence alone does not prove nesting, and abundance on a Lebanese beach should not be extrapolated to the Gulf or North Africa. Ecological role and conservation As an invertebrate predator it forms part of coastal food webs, with survival depending on both feeding and resting habitat. The global assessment changed to Vulnerable, VU, in 2024, a status retained by AviList 2026. Older pages that still display Least Concern are outdated for this purpose. Pressures include coastal habitat loss and degradation, disturbance and hunting along migration routes. Maintaining connected mudflats and high-tide refuges, and avoiding repeated approaches or vehicle disturbance, are practical conservation priorities. Global conservation status does not itself establish local hunting law. References AviList 2026 — Pluvialis squatarola. articles.title: Grey Wagtail
articles.body: Grey Wagtail Motacilla cinerea — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and recognition The Grey Wagtail, Motacilla cinerea, belongs to Motacillidae, the wagtail and pipit family. Its name describes only part of its appearance: the back is grey, but the undertail is conspicuously yellow and the tail is extremely long relative to the body. Legs are pinkish brown. A breeding male has a black throat; females have a paler throat, sometimes with variable black. Young birds are less vivid, with a pale throat and weaker yellow on the breast. These characters change with age and season, so throat colour alone is not a reliable year-round sexing method. Distinguishing similar birds Yellow undertail feathers help separate it from a White Wagtail. Distinguishing it from yellow wagtails requires closer comparison: look for the combination of a grey back, proportionately longer tail and pale legs, rather than yellow plumage alone. A pale wing stripe may show in flight. Feeding around rocks and water margins also provides a clue, but habitat never replaces identification: other wagtails can visit the same stream. Habitat, food and behaviour Breeding birds are associated with streams and rivers, especially where rocky margins provide insects and sheltered nesting places. Outside the season they also use slower water, ponds, lakes and channels; some move downhill to milder areas. They collect insects and other small invertebrates along edges and exposed surfaces, sometimes catching prey in the air. A field study in Cyprus recorded flies and dragonflies among nestling foods, illustrating the connection with insects around water. Breeding and annual cycle The nest occupies shelter near water, such as a rock or wall recess, a space beneath a bridge or roots in a bank. Suitable nestboxes may be accepted. British records give a typical clutch of five eggs, incubation of about 12–13 days and a nestling period of roughly 14–15 days. These reference durations vary; the breeding season is established locally. Successful nesting requires food and a site protected from flooding and repeated disturbance. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Residence and migration differ across Arab countries. Jordan’s checklist describes a winter visitor and a less common passage migrant. Syria’s 2025 checklist documents uncommon resident breeding in the northern coastal region, together with widespread wintering and passage in different regions. The Moroccan checklist published in 2010 records resident breeders and winter visitors. Qatar e-Nature, by contrast, describes a rare passage migrant. An October observation in the Levant may therefore fit passage or the beginning of winter presence. Occasional Gulf records should not be turned into a claim of common wintering throughout the Gulf. Kuwait’s endorsed checklist, updated in September 2026, records uncommon passage and scarce winter presence. Ecology and conservation The bird depends on connections between water, its margins and invertebrate food. Maintaining suitable flow, varied banks and sheltered nesting places benefits its habitat. Water pollution, channel deterioration and altered banks can threaten habitat and prey; severe winter weather can affect some populations. Its global category is Least Concern, not a guarantee that every local population is stable. Regular monitoring is useful, but a single wagtail sighting is not, by itself, a certificate of clean water. articles.title: Neighbours in Poland, migration routes 3,750 kilometres apart
articles.body: Andrey Gulivanov / Wikimedia Commons They leave from almost the same area and head for Africa, but their routes are less alike than we might expect. Five male European honey-buzzards breed at sites no more than 60 kilometres apart, yet their migration routes diverge until they are separated by 3,750 kilometres. The contrast emerged from a study published in the Journal of Ornithology, after researchers tracked the birds in northeastern Poland between 2018 and 2024. They used four migration corridors: Gibraltar, the Apennines in Italy, the Balkans and the Bosporus. Mirski et al. / Journal of Ornithology, 2026 More strikingly, their wintering areas were much closer together than their routes, with no more than 575 kilometres between them. Neighbours at departure, widely separated paths across continents, then relatively close destinations. The same bird can change its route The differences were not only between birds. Some individuals changed their routes from year to year, taking detours around obstacles such as mountains, seas and deserts. Mirski et al. / Journal of Ornithology, 2026 Variation in migration timing was most apparent during the spring return, with clear differences in arrival dates at the breeding grounds. The researchers see the results as evidence of flexibility and individuality in route choice. The small sample of five males documents this flexibility among the tracked birds and opens the way to studying it on a larger scale. Why is the shortest route not always the best? Earlier research helps explain some of the reasons for detours in this species. In an independent study tracking 62 journeys by 12 adult birds, researchers found that seasonal detours through West Africa allow the birds to take advantage of favourable winds, reducing the energy cost of crossing the Sahara. The shortest distance on a map is not necessarily the least costly in the air. The European honey-buzzard, whose scientific name is Pernis apivorus, is a broad-winged, long-tailed raptor that spends the winter in tropical Africa. It searches bees’ and wasps’ nests for larvae, and large numbers may gather during autumn migration before crossing the Mediterranean. Yet behind a flock that seems to be heading in one direction, tracking devices reveal different stories: each bird has its own route, and that route may change from one journey to the next. Sources: Mirski, Komar and Tumiel study in the Journal of Ornithology; Independent research on wind effects in the Journal of Animal Ecology; Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB)

articles.title: Macho hunting… when some look for their manhood among bird carcasses!
articles.body: Photos received by the Anti-Poaching Unit team, October 2026. Among the strangest sights we see on social media are photographs of people standing proudly in front of dozens of dead birds, lining them up on cars or spreading them across the ground, holding their shotguns with triumphant expressions, as though they had returned from a historic battle in which they had achieved a great victory! More amusing still, some of them use their companions’ game, or pool the take of several hunters, and sometimes even borrow birds from other people’s refrigerators to complete the picture of heroism they seek! It seems that, for some, heroism can now be borrowed, and even stored in refrigerators! But what kind of heroism is this? And what kind of manhood needs dozens of carcasses to prove its existence? Hunting is a sport of courage, patience, skill and challenge, founded on knowledge of nature and respect for it, and on an ethical code that makes hunters responsible for their actions. Sustainable hunting is a culture that protects wildlife and ensures that the sport continues for future generations. A professional hunter is known for his experience, conduct and respect for nature. He knows his worth well and does not need to display bird carcasses to convince others of his skill. Adonis Alkhateeb, Editor-in-Chief, during an anti-poaching field activity in Lebanon, October 2026. As for our friend who needs this spectacle to feel important, perhaps he is trying to make up for a status he lacks, or gain admiration he cannot earn through a genuine achievement. Let us imagine for a moment that the bird carries a shotgun, just like the hunter who fires at it. Would we see the same display? Would our friend stand with his chest puffed out before an opponent equally capable of fighting back? It is very easy to manufacture heroism when the other side is unable to defend itself! Sadly, these displays damage the reputation of respectable hunters and turn a time-honoured sport into scenes of killing and boasting, degrading life and dismissing the values of compassion affirmed by ethics and religious teachings. Even Lebanese Law No. 580/2004, in Article 8, expressly prohibits displaying hunted game outside cars and on public roads. What a disgrace! Birds that have travelled thousands of kilometres and overcome storms and dangers during migration end their lives as part of an absurd spectacle, while the man behind it waits for a few likes and comments! More ironic still, some even boast about game they did not hunt! Gentlemen, hunting is about ethics and responsibility, and respect for one’s quarry is part of a hunter’s self-respect. And anyone who convinces others that he is strong, brave and important should ask himself how real that strength and courage are. Manhood is not measured by the number of birds we kill, and a hunter’s worth shows in his ethics and respect for life. As for anyone searching for his manhood among bird carcasses, he would do better to look for it somewhere else!

articles.title: Kentish Plover
articles.body: Kentish Plover Anarhynchus alexandrinus Identity and identification Kentish Plover is a small coastal bird of Charadriidae, order Charadriiformes. It is called الزقزاق الإسكندري in Arabic and Gravelot à collier interrompu in French. Its scientific name is Anarhynchus alexandrinus; older references place it in Charadrius. About 15–18 cm long, it has sandy upperparts, white underparts, a slender black bill and dark legs. Its most striking breast character is the gap between two lateral patches, instead of a continuous black band. Breeding males have black head and breast markings and reddish colouring on the head and nape; females are browner and less contrasting. Pale feather edges give juveniles a scaled appearance above. Ages and sexes become less distinct in autumn, so a distant photograph does not justify confident assignment. A white wingbar shows in flight. Non-breeding Little Ringed Plover requires care because its breast band can also be incomplete: eye-ring, bill, legs and wings complete the comparison. Habitat, food and behaviour Sandy or shingly beaches, saltflats, saltpans, saline lake margins and estuaries provide habitat, generally with low, sparse vegetation. Apparently empty sand contains food, resting places and sometimes exceptionally well-camouflaged nests. Suitable inland sites are used too; the species is not confined to the sea edge. Its food includes insects, spiders, worms, small crustaceans and molluscs, varying with locality and season. It picks prey from the surface and damp sand, alternating short runs with searching pauses. Outside breeding, groups may join other waders. Looking across the whole flock reveals the different small-scale feeding habitats shared by its members. Breeding and development The usual clutch is three eggs, occasionally four, in a shallow ground depression. A BirdLife Cyprus review gives incubation of 24–27 days and flight at 27–31 days after hatching. Both parents incubate. Downy chicks move soon after hatching but need protection and care before they can fly. These figures describe development, not a single breeding calendar for every Arab coast. Walking chicks are not necessarily abandoned: approaching may separate them from their parents. Nesting areas are best protected by leaving them undisturbed, rather than seeking nests or exposing eggs for photographs. Range and Arab occurrence The range spans substantial parts of Eurasia, North Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Northern populations move south in winter while others remain closer to their breeding areas. Oman’s official list records a common breeder and abundant passage migrant and winter visitor. The 2026 Lebanon guide instead describes a rare-to-scarce passage migrant and rare summer visitor, with occasional non-breeders in June and July on the coast and at Palm Islands, Aammiq and Lake Qaraoun. This does not establish Lebanese breeding or regular wintering. Kuwait’s committee list describes a common resident breeder, another clear indication that the Lebanese pattern does not represent the whole region. What November means The distinction matters in November. Suitable Omani coasts may support winter arrivals alongside regional birds, while a late Lebanese observation should not automatically become evidence of winter residency. Repeat visits recording tides and numbers are more useful than assuming one seasonal pattern everywhere. Check breast and wing characters on each bird rather than relying only on its sandy appearance. Conservation and responsible observation The global category is Least Concern (LC), although local populations may decline without a change in that category. Pressures include loss of natural shores, pollution, disturbance and illegal hunting. Vehicles, dogs and recreational groups crossing open ground can make otherwise suitable resting or nesting habitat unusable. Respect closures and safe distances, keep dogs restrained, and never chase flocks into flight. Quiet ground above the waterline matters alongside wet feeding habitat. articles.title: Laughing Dove
articles.body: Laughing Dove Spilopelia senegalensis — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and identification The Laughing Dove, Spilopelia senegalensis, is a small member of the pigeon and dove family, Columbidae, in the order Columbiformes. Also called Palm Dove, it is familiar around many Arab towns, farms and oases. At approximately 25–27 cm long, with a wingspan of about 40–45 cm, it combines a small head, slender body and relatively long tail. Adults have warm pinkish-brown head and breast, a browner back and blue-grey areas on the wings. A patch of black spotting on a rusty background across the lower fore-neck is especially useful. White on the outer tail becomes conspicuous when the tail opens. The sexes are similar, and small colour differences are unreliable for identifying a single bird’s sex. Young birds are duller and have a weak or absent spotted neck patch. Eurasian Collared Dove is larger and paler, with a simple dark half-collar behind the neck. European Turtle Dove shows more strongly patterned, dark-centred upperwing feathers and a striped neck patch. Laughing Dove has a plainer upperwing and longer-looking tail. These characters are best assessed together, rather than relying on size in an isolated photograph. Its soft, rolling series of coos gives rise to the English name; the bird is not expressing human laughter. Habitat, food and behaviour It occupies open scrub, lightly wooded country, orchards, cultivated land, gardens and settlements. In arid landscapes, watered gardens and oases provide food and vegetation for nesting. It also uses built structures, including sheltered ledges and plant containers. Dense buildings without food or nesting opportunities are less informative than the presence of suitable small patches of habitat. Most food is collected on the ground. Small seeds and grains predominate, with some fruit, other plant material and insects. Birds walk and pick up individual food items, often as a pair or in small groups. Larger gatherings can form at concentrated food or water. Flight is quick, and a startled bird may rise abruptly. Pairs maintain breeding territories even where many birds occupy the same neighbourhood. Breeding and life cycle Courtship combines repeated cooing, body movements and display flights. Both partners contribute to the simple twig platform, usually in a tree or shrub but sometimes on a building. Two white eggs are usual. Both parents incubate and feed the young, which initially receive nutrient-rich crop milk. Incubation generally lasts about two weeks; young leave the nest roughly two weeks after hatching, with variation between populations and studies. They may still depend on their parents after leaving. Breeding opportunities can recur within a year. In Saudi Arabia breeding is documented over a broad season, with much activity from late winter into summer. A Taif study recorded the onset in mid-February. Egyptian and Maghreb populations also breed seasonally, but local conditions matter: a documented Moroccan nest with eggs in August illustrates why a single narrow calendar is unsuitable. Distribution and regional seasonality Its extensive range covers much of Africa and parts of western, central and southern Asia; western Australian populations are introduced. It is principally resident, with dispersal and local movements associated with conditions rather than obligatory long-distance seasonal migration. In Arabia it breeds widely in suitable settled and cultivated habitats, including Saudi Arabia, Oman and Kuwait. In the Mashriq, Lebanon has an established resident breeding population. Egypt supports resident breeders in settled and cultivated areas, with field studies in Sharkia and Sinai. In the Maghreb it breeds in orchards, towns and oases; its expansion across Morocco and other North African areas is well documented. Ecology and conservation A mainly seed-eating bird, it is also prey within terrestrial food webs. Global status is Least Concern. Local nesting losses can result from predation, disturbance or nest abandonment; indiscriminate shooting is another recorded pressure. Maintaining shrubs, orchard habitat and quiet nesting places benefits birds alongside people. Leave active nests undisturbed and enjoy the calls without approaching the birds. articles.title: Lebanon's Hunting Law 580/2004: Why an open season does not authorize every hunt
articles.body: A statutory guide to permits, protected birds, prohibited methods and no-hunting areas. Raouche Rocks in Beirut, Lebanon An announcement opening a hunting season does not override the underlying legislation. Lebanon's Hunting Law 580, dated 25 February 2004 and published in the Official Gazette on 4 March 2004, establishes lasting rules on eligible species, licensing, prohibited methods and protected places. Article 4 treats wild resident and migratory birds and mammals as protected unless they are designated as permissible quarry under applicable conditions. The season dates are determined through a separate implementing measure; they are not a general permission to shoot any bird. Article 6 requires a hunting licence issued by the Ministry of Environment, supported by the relevant firearms authorization and third-party liability insurance. Article 8 prohibits hunting in cities, villages and nature reserves, and includes a buffer of at least 500 metres from dwellings, places of worship and public or private facilities. Article 9 prohibits trapping nets, birdlime, other indiscriminate devices, spotlights and recorded bird calls used to attract quarry, alongside additional restrictions. Article 10 protects wild nests, eggs and young throughout the year. Responsible hunting therefore involves more than observing a calendar. This article explains the original 2004 law, not a newly enacted 2026 law. For any specific legal action, consult subsequent amendments, regulations and current official decisions. Source: Lebanon's Ministry of Environment, Hunting Law 580/2004, Articles 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 10. Original statute at the official source

articles.title: Leen Araji: Equestrian Champion and Mental Math Champion
articles.body: Leen Araji — jumping champion and mental-math talent. Equestrian sport answers not to age but to the will to challenge. Sayd meets Leen Araji — a Lebanese jumping champion and a world-ranked mental math talent. Equestrian sport is not subject to the will of age, but to the will to challenge and to strong resolve. That is why it is a kind of special arithmetic, with special equations, that reaches its goals in a leap of light. Leen Araji is an equestrian champion with a Lebanese signature — and a mental math champion with a global one. Sayd held this conversation with her. She said in the interview: I was introduced to horses at the age of 10, trained by my cousin Sheikh Omran Araji, who was hard on me so I would achieve the best performance. The Araji family has long been known for loving and keeping horses. Horses give confidence and strengthen personal force. My first jump was in a Beirut competition. I felt no fear because I was determined not to fear; the feeling was beautiful, and I sensed I had to clear every fence the same way. We must calculate every step — in a horse jump or in a leap of life. That idea strengthened my mental math and my win in “Genius Map”: I ranked third in the Beqaa and fourth worldwide. I also want to become a world equestrian champion and to compete outside Lebanon. A horse feels the rider’s fear, and for that reason may turn against them and throw them. A rider should try several horses to understand their mistakes better and correct them through experience. Of course I would love to have a farm. I know enough about the horse world, but I do not enjoy training horses myself. In training we jump at heights of 100 cm; in competitions, between 60 and 90 cm. To date I have entered nine competitions and won seven of them. I do not have my own horse. I love “Doha” because she was the first mare I trained on and still do; if I had my own horse I would name him “Reem.” Outside equestrian sport my hobbies are swimming and boxing. If I marry one day, I will make my husband love horses. I could never eat horse meat — quite simply, I do not eat meat. I love competing in all Arab countries, but I lean toward Jordan. I have fallen from the horse more than once; once I broke my arm and stopped training for four months — but nothing keeps me from continuing, as the saying goes: “If we don’t fall, we don’t learn.” I love both: math and horses. A rider’s heart loves everything.

articles.title: Marsh Sandpiper
articles.body: Marsh Sandpiper Tringa stagnatilis — a slender migrant of shallow wetlands Name and classification The Marsh Sandpiper, Tringa stagnatilis, belongs to the family Scolopacidae and order Charadriiformes in AviList 2026. The Lebanese guide calls it Darijat al-mustanqaʿat; Kuwaiti references also use names meaning marsh or wetland sandpiper. These regional names identify the same notably slender wader. Its breeding range extends across parts of eastern Europe, Russia and Kazakhstan to north-eastern China, while wintering populations occupy a broad belt from Africa through southern Asia to Australia. Field identification Its straight black bill is exceptionally fine, its long legs greenish or yellowish, and its slender neck gives it an upright, graceful stance. Winter adults have pale grey upperparts, white underparts and a pale face; breeding plumage gains darker spotting. The sexes look similar. Juveniles are browner, with pale margins to the back feathers. In flight, white extends from the rump up the back and the feet project beyond the tail. Common Greenshank is more heavily built, with a thicker, slightly upturned bill. Bill structure considered together with leg length also helps separate it from Wood Sandpiper. Habitat, food and behaviour It uses lake margins, marshes, pools and flooded grasslands, feeding in shallow water and exposed mud. Inland wetlands are particularly important, although coastal sites also support migrants and winter visitors. It takes insects and their larvae, molluscs and other small invertebrates, and its long legs allow it to wade deeper than smaller, shorter-legged waders. Birds search while walking, alone or in gatherings that can include other species. Suitable feeding patches shift with water levels: an entirely flooded basin does not necessarily offer the same opportunities as its shallow margins. Breeding and life cycle In its northern breeding range it selects open marshes and wet grassland, nesting from late April into June according to locality and weather. The nest lies low among vegetation or on a small rise and is lined with dry grass. Pairs may occur in loose aggregations, sometimes close to other waders. The Romanian Ornithological Society describes clutches of three to five eggs, incubated by both sexes. Timing varies across the breeding range. Its winter presence in the Gulf belongs to a different stage of the annual cycle, centred on feeding, survival and preparation for the next migration. Both parents continue caring for the young after hatching. The scientific account of Kazakhstan’s birds records hatching in June and early July, followed by the onset of flight in late July within that geographical range. Juveniles there migrate later in summer, after adults have begun leaving. This sequence follows development from parental care to flight and migration without turning the Kazakh calendar into a fixed chick age or a universal breeding schedule. Arab distribution and November The 2026 Lebanese guide treats it as a scarce passage migrant and very rare winter visitor, using the coast, estuaries, islands and wetlands. Kuwait’s endorsed national list classifies it as a common passage migrant and winter visitor, as does the Oman database. In Saudi Arabia it is an uncommon passage migrant and winter visitor; the national reference specifies winter occurrence from November to February. Egypt and the Nile Valley form part of its African range; range lists also document it in other Arab countries of the Levant, Arabian Peninsula and North Africa. Early November is therefore an appropriate winter observation period in Kuwait and Oman, whereas a Lebanese winter record merits careful documentation. Abundance within a country varies with water, food and disturbance. Conservation and responsible observation Its current global category is Least Concern, LC. Pressures include wetland drainage, pollution, altered management and disturbance. Feeding links aquatic invertebrates with higher levels of the food web, while conservation benefits from protecting a network of passage and wintering sites. Observers should wait at an existing viewing edge rather than follow a bird through its feeding area, and stop approaching if it repeatedly moves away or interrupts feeding. Record the date, location and number present, ideally with a side view showing the bill and legs; these details are more useful than a close image obtained by chasing it. articles.title: Northern Shoveler: a filtering bill and an autumn journey through Arab wetlands
articles.body: Northern Shoveler Among the ducks gathering beside autumn ponds, the Northern Shoveler often announces its identity before its colours are clear: a long bill widening into a spatula. Rather than simply digging into mud, it filters tiny food items from the water. Its seasonal return offers a way to understand the value of shallow wetlands, not just another name to add to a sightings list. Identity card Arabic: أبو مجرف; also مجرفي المنقار English: Northern Shoveler French: Canard souchet Scientific name: Spatula clypeata; older sources use Anas clypeata Order and family: Anseriformes; Anatidae Length: approximately 44–51 cm; wingspan approximately 69–84 cm Habitat: shallow freshwater or brackish ponds, marshes and lakes Arab-world status: chiefly passage migrant and winter visitor, with rare local breeding records Global conservation category: Least Concern (LC); scientific name and taxonomy follow AviList v2026 [1] Why it matters this season Arab wetlands gain importance as ducks move from northern breeding grounds towards their winter quarters. In Saudi Arabia, winter presence extends from October to March. On the western flyway, Danish ringing records document some birds reaching Morocco in October. These are examples of different migration routes, not a single arrival date for every Arab country. [6] [12] Different statuses across the Arab world In Tunisia, a winter 2020–2021 survey, published in 2024, confirms its presence. In Algeria, researchers published a June 2019 record from Sebkhet El-Mahmel of a pair accompanied by eight young. “Winter visitor” therefore describes the predominant pattern without excluding all local breeding; that record does not establish widespread residency either. [9] [10] In Egypt, historical assessments of Lake Nasser include the species among wintering ducks. This documents the site’s role, not a current population count. In Palestine, the Wildlife Society’s checklist describes it as very common in winter and on passage. Inclusion in a national list does not mean equal abundance at every pond, or that the species breeds there. [11] [8] Rare breeding has been recorded in Qatif, Saudi Arabia. In the UAE: locally common to very common on passage and in winter, occasionally in summer. An individual remaining through summer is not, by itself, evidence of nesting. [6] [7] The bill first, then the plumage A male in bright plumage has a dark green head, white breast and chestnut flanks. The wing shows a pale blue area and a green speculum. These colours are useful, but the bill’s widened tip remains the most dependable feature when poor light conceals the head’s sheen. [2] Females and immature birds are mottled brown; a moulting male may look more similar to them. Brown markings alone do not establish that a bird is female. When comparing it with a female Mallard, consider the conspicuously expanded bill together with head and wing structure. Colour or a distant photograph is not enough to assign sex and age confidently. [3] Small food, distinctive behaviour Fine plates along the bill edges form a filter for aquatic invertebrates and seeds. Birds sometimes swim in circles or sweep their bills from side to side while feeding. This specialisation helps explain their association with productive shallows. Finding one on a treatment pond or in turbid water does not establish that the water is clean or safe for people. [4] From nesting to the next migration Most breeding occurs in northern temperate Eurasia and North America. The female makes a ground nest concealed by vegetation, lines it with down, incubates the eggs and tends the young. BTO data give a typical clutch of 9–11 eggs, around 22–23 days of incubation and flight at roughly 40–45 days. These are approximate biological intervals, not a fixed calendar for every population. [5] Ducklings hatch covered in down and can swim soon afterwards, but still need cover and care. After breeding, plumage is renewed; males become temporarily flightless while their wing feathers are replaced. Birds subsequently gather and move towards wintering areas. A quiet bird seen in summer must therefore be distinguished from evidence of a nest or brood. [4] Its value, and responsible watching The Shoveler illustrates the diversity of feeding strategies within a wetland, linking tiny aquatic organisms with the bird food web. Its conservation requires connected feeding and resting places, rather than protection of an attractive image in isolation from habitat. Global Least Concern status does not guarantee that every local gathering is secure or that draining a small pond has no consequences. [13] Use binoculars from a fixed position and do not flush a flock for a photograph. Record the date, location, number and behaviour: these details help distinguish passage from repeated occupation. Hunting status depends on the rules applying to the country, site and season; it cannot be inferred from the conservation category or the label “wild duck”. articles.title: Northern Wheatear in the Arab world: an autumn traveller of open ground
articles.body: Northern Wheatear A small bird pauses on a stone, drops to the ground for prey and returns to a lookout. When it flies, white flashes across the rump and tail. This is a familiar Northern Wheatear scene during migration, when open ground across the Arab world becomes a stop along a much longer journey between breeding and wintering areas. Identification card Arabic name: الأبلق الشمالي English name: Northern Wheatear French name: Traquet motteux Scientific name: Oenanthe oenanthe Family: Muscicapidae Length: approximately 14–16 cm Habitat: bare ground, short grass, stony plains and sparsely vegetated slopes Arab-world occurrence: widespread passage migrant; breeds in parts of the Levant, with limited winter occurrence in some areas Global conservation status: Least Concern (LC) From the Maghreb to Arabia Ringing data in the Eurasian-African Migration Atlas connect April and September–October encounters in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia with several European breeding regions. A passing wheatear cannot therefore simply be described as a bird from one particular country. A recovered ring establishes a connection between documented locations, rather than necessarily revealing every part of the journey. In the Levant, passage overlaps with local breeding. Lebanon's checklist documents summer breeding, especially at 1,500–2,500 metres, autumn passage from early August to late November, and smaller numbers in winter. In Saudi Arabia, Saudipedia describes a common passage migrant that does not breed in the country. The comparison matters: occurrence in an Arab country does not itself establish residency or wintering status. Most populations travel to wintering areas south of the Sahara. Tracking research on North American breeders has shown that even populations very far from Africa reach that continent by different routes. This does not make every wheatear seen in the Levant an Alaskan bird. An individual's origin needs its own evidence. Why autumn brings it into view Southward movement reaches North Africa from August and becomes conspicuous in September, while the last birds leave Europe during October. Local observations from Dhahran in eastern Saudi Arabia include September and October, as well as spring passage. These are regional seasonal windows, not fixed arrival dates for every country and year. A bird may pause in a short-grass field, on stony ground or beside a farm. A few days' presence does not show that its journey has ended. Recording the length of a stay, behaviour and observation date is more useful: passage, wintering and breeding are different situations that one photograph cannot establish. Recognising more than the spring male A breeding male usually has a grey back, black mask and dark wings. The female is browner and less contrasting, without the same bold black mask. In autumn, sandy or warm tones soften the appearance of many individuals, unlike the sharply patterned spring males familiar from illustrations. Assess the upright stance, legs, face and wing pattern, then the black-and-white tail when it becomes visible naturally. A white rump alone is insufficient because other wheatears share it. Nor does an overall brown colour in a distant photograph reliably establish sex or age. Document several features and leave uncertain identifications open. Small prey and a sheltered nest Its diet consists mainly of insects and other small invertebrates, with some berries. Sparse vegetation leaves room to locate and reach prey. Near a stone or low perch, the pauses and short movements to the ground can be watched without attracting the bird with food. In breeding areas, the nest is concealed in a cavity or rock crevice. BTO data give five to six eggs as a typical clutch; a British nesting calendar should not be transferred directly to Arab mountain habitats. A bird standing on a rock in October is not evidence of a nest beneath it. Conservation and responsible observation Least Concern describes global extinction risk and does not rule out local declines. European monitoring shows that a wide geographical range does not remove the need for habitat protection and continued surveys. The category also does not determine hunting law, which must be checked with the relevant national authority. Stay far enough away for the bird to keep feeding. Do not flush it to reveal the tail or follow it towards a nesting cavity. Record date, habitat, elevation and behaviour. Leaving a stopover undisturbed helps protect the journey briefly made visible by this small traveller.
