articles.title: Oman regulates reserve visits and camping
articles.body: Khor Rori, part of the khor reserves along the Salalah coast. Six decisions regulate visitor entry, camping and overnight stays to protect wildlife Oman's Environment Authority has issued six decisions regulating the management of nature reserves. They cover visitor entry, camping, overnight stays and documentary filming, and specify activities prohibited to protect wildlife. The decisions were published in the Official Gazette on 25 October 2026 and take effect on 26 October 2026. The decisions cover Khor Salalah Nature Reserve, Al Jabal Al Gharbi Nature Reserve, Al Dhahirah Nature Reserve, the khor reserves along the Salalah coast, Al Buraimi Oasis Nature Reserve and Ras Al Shajar Nature Reserve. Khor Rori and the sandbar separating it from the sea. Before visiting or camping The provisions require permits to enter the reserves concerned, camp or stay overnight. The rules for Al Jabal Al Gharbi, Al Dhahirah, Al Buraimi Oasis and Ras Al Shajar reserves also make roaming and mountain hiking subject to a permit. Applications must be submitted to the Environment Authority using the designated form. The competent body must decide on an application within 30 days of receiving it complete, making advance trip planning and completion of the necessary procedures important. Specific exemptions from the entry permit include reserve residents and their first-degree relatives, school pupils on educational trips, official government delegations, and specified military, security, government and academic personnel performing the duties set out in the provisions. These exemptions concern entry only and do not automatically waive permits for other activities. What about photography? The provisions require a permit for photography or filming intended to produce documentaries or promote the reserve. Personal photography is not mentioned in this clause, which specifies the purposes for which a permit is required. The khor reserves along the Salalah coast include Khor Rori, where the coastal landscape, water and natural habitats meet. It is shown in the two photographs accompanying this article. No hunting; keep to designated routes The provisions prohibit hunting and the use of weapons, laying poison, and collecting fossils, archaeological objects, stones or other items found in the reserve. They also prohibit driving vehicles off designated routes, damaging trees and plants, polluting water sources, and introducing alien or invasive wildlife species. Other activities require permits, including lighting fires outside designated areas, studies and research, and collecting wildlife samples. An entry permit does not replace the permits required for these activities. The decisions include fees and schedules of offences and administrative fines. Details vary by reserve and activity. Anyone planning a visit or camping trip should therefore check the provisions for the intended reserve and confirm the permits and fees applicable to their trip. articles.title: Protecting Autumn Migratory Birds in Lebanon: A Field Partnership Since 2017, Al-Khatib Affirms the Sustainable Hunter’s Role
articles.body: Members of the Anti-Poaching Unit with birds rescued during a joint patrol — Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching Beirut — Sayd The Committee Against Bird Slaughter — known as CABS — announced the launch of its autumn campaign to protect migratory birds in Lebanon, in cooperation with its local partner the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching — MECSHAP, with a focus on protecting migratory raptors and combating hunting with nets and birdlime (lime sticks / glue traps), according to its announcement published on 8 September 2026. In a statement to Sayd, Adonis Al-Khatib, head of the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching, said: The Anti-Poaching Unit (APU) at MECSHAP, in cooperation with CABS, is preparing to carry out the autumn anti-poaching camp in Lebanon, as part of a field partnership ongoing since 2017, which began after CABS contacted MECSHAP through the Society for the Protection of Nature in Lebanon (SPNL). He added: “CABS works against illegal bird killing in a number of European countries, while its cooperation with APU has been a unique experience, as it was CABS’s first such experience with sustainable hunters taking part directly in anti-poaching. The experience has shown that the sustainable hunter is a true partner in protecting migratory birds and confronting violations in Lebanon.” From the daily field life of the Anti-Poaching Unit team: a break to prepare food outdoors. He continued: “Work during the spring and autumn camps focuses on monitoring and documenting violations involving birdlime, nets, night hunting, and indiscriminate killing of migratory birds, in coordination with the security agencies, the Lebanese Army, and the competent judiciary. The unit is entering this autumn’s camp at a high level of readiness, supported by a wide network of hunters and citizens who supply the operations team with reports, photos, and precise locations.” Source: Committee Against Bird Slaughter announcement — 8 September 2026, and Adonis Al-Khatib’s statement to Sayd.

articles.title: Purple Heron
articles.body: Purple Heron Ardea purpurea Identity and identification Purple Heron Ardea purpurea belongs to Ardeidae. More slender than Grey Heron, it has a long neck, pointed bill and adult chestnut-brown plumage with dark neck stripes. Juveniles are browner and less contrasting. Like other herons, it retracts its neck in flight, unlike extended-necked storks. It is placed in the order Pelecaniformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Dense reed marshes, shallow water, lakesides and channels provide habitat. Concealed among plants or waiting still, it takes fish, amphibians, insects and other small animals. Reed-coloured plumage and immobility can hide a large bird surprisingly effectively. Breeding and parental care A nest of reed stems and twigs stands within dense wet cover, sometimes in shrubs. BTO gives three to five eggs and shared incubation around 25–30 days. Both parents feed young, which may climb vegetation before full flight. Leaving the nest platform does not mean independence. Range and Arab occurrence Its range spans parts of Europe, Africa and Asia. Arab wetlands serve breeding, passage or wintering functions according to location. Lebanon’s updated checklist describes coastal, island and inland passage; frequent sightings alone do not establish breeding. Seasonality and observation Lebanese passage extends from mid-March to mid-June and, in larger numbers, early August to late November. November therefore falls within expected autumn occurrence. Neck, bill and wing details distinguish Grey Heron without entering reeds. Ecological role and conservation Reed cover, water and food are essential. Drainage, reed burning, pollution and disturbance are pressures. Reed management should respect bird seasons and retain safe areas; cosmetic pond edges cannot replace the functions of a complete marsh. articles.title: Redwing
articles.body: Redwing Turdus iliacus Identity, life and distribution Redwing Turdus iliacus is a relatively small thrush with a conspicuous pale eyebrow and reddish flanks. Red also shows beneath the wings in flight; its name does not mean that the entire wing is red. Birds move in response to fruit and other food supplies, and winter visitor numbers can vary greatly between years. Fields, hedges and fruit-bearing trees form complementary parts of its non-breeding habitat. It nests in northern parts of its range. BTO gives a typical clutch of four or five eggs. British breeding figures do not describe its global distribution, and winter occurrence does not establish local nesting. Retaining fruit-bearing vegetation and quiet resting places helps visiting birds. Photographs showing the eyebrow and flanks aid separation from other thrushes. It occurs in the non-breeding season in parts of the Maghreb, including Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia. articles.title: Rock Dove
articles.body: Rock Dove Columba livia Identity and identification Rock Dove Columba livia belongs to Columbidae and is the wild ancestor of domestic pigeons. Typical wild-type birds are grey with two black wing bars, a pale rump and green-purple neck gloss. Feral city pigeons can share this appearance, so colour alone cannot establish genetically wild ancestry. It is placed in the order Columbiformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Wild birds nest on coastal and inland cliffs and in caves, feeding on seeds and grain in open country. Domestic and feral forms exploit buildings and human food. Flocks travel to feeding and watering places; dependence on people varies among populations. Breeding and parental care Usually two eggs lie in a simple nest on a ledge or sheltered site. Both parents incubate for about 18–19 days and feed chicks crop milk, progressively adding plant food. Repeated broods are possible when conditions permit; urban productivity cannot be assumed for every wild cliff population. Range and Arab occurrence Its native wild range includes the Mediterranean, North Africa and Middle East. Lebanon’s checklist describes a cliff-nesting breeding resident. Feral pigeons are widespread around Arab cities. Distinguishing these categories matters when describing natural habitats or counting wild populations. Seasonality and observation Usually resident where rock sites and food persist, it can be observed in November. Habitat, behaviour and distance from settlements should accompany plumage notes, while mixed ancestry remains possible. A single photograph should not be labelled proof of genetically pure wild origin. Ecological role and conservation It consumes seeds and supplies prey for several raptors. Domestic introgression threatens original wild populations, alongside cliff disturbance and habitat loss. Urban pigeon management differs from protecting wild ancestry; avoiding indiscriminate feeding also improves conditions for urban flocks. articles.title: Ruddy Turnstone
articles.body: Ruddy Turnstone Arenaria interpres Name and identity Ruddy Turnstone, Arenaria interpres, belongs to Scolopacidae within Charadriiformes. Lebanon’s 2026 guide and Kuwait’s bird reference use the Arabic name Qunburat al-maa. Despite that name it is not a lark; the scientific name is the clearest reference for photographs and records. AviList 2026 retains it, and the French name is Tournepierre à collier. Its character is most apparent on the shore: a short-legged bird working among pebbles and stranded seaweed, pushing a small object aside to expose what lies beneath. The English name combines its colourful summer appearance with this stone-turning habit. Plumage and identification It is compact, with orange legs and a short, sturdy bill slightly upturned at the tip. Breeding plumage combines chestnut, black and white, with bold face and breast markings. Females are generally less vivid than males, but sex assignment needs a clear view rather than a single colour in a distant photograph. Winter upperparts become browner, while white underparts and the dark breast pattern remain. Juveniles have pale or rusty feather margins that make the back appear scaly. Flight reveals strong white markings on wings, back and rump, with a dark tail band. This combination separates it from nearby sandpipers and plovers; stone-turning behaviour alone does not establish identity. Food and habitat It visits rocky, shingle and sandy shores, mudflats and estuaries, sometimes stopping beside inland waters on migration. Moving stones, shells and seaweed exposes crustaceans, molluscs, insects and other invertebrates. Its varied diet changes with place and season, making natural strandline material part of feeding habitat rather than mere rubbish. Outside nesting it gathers in groups, sometimes with other waders. Tides shape movement between food and rest. Birds need accessible feeding ground and quieter higher ground when water covers it. Their consumption of invertebrates places them within coastal food webs. Breeding and development It nests in open Arctic and subarctic country in a ground scrape lined with plant material. The usual clutch is four eggs; BTO records three to five and typical incubation of 22–24 days, mainly by the female with occasional male participation. Downy chicks are mobile and gather food, with parents accompanying and protecting them. Leaving the nest site does not mean they can fly: the reference gives about 19–21 days to that stage. After breeding, birds move to warmer coasts; some non-breeders may remain in wintering regions through summer. Arab occurrence and season Arab coasts form part of its passage and non-breeding network. Lebanon’s 2026 guide describes scarce passage and winter visitation on shores and islands, rarely at inland lakes. Kuwait records common passage, uncommon wintering and scarce summer occurrence; Oman’s database describes abundant passage and winter visitation. November is therefore suitable for watching on Arab shores, but expected numbers vary geographically. Occurrence on a Gulf beach does not imply equal abundance in the Levant, and summer presence alone does not prove nesting. Place, count and date make records useful for understanding local seasonality. Conservation and watching The 2024 Red List assessment classifies Ruddy Turnstone as Near Threatened, NT, with a decreasing trend; AviList 2026 repeats that category. Least Concern on some older pages is not the latest global status. Coastal habitat loss, oil pollution and disturbance affect feeding and resting sites. For photography, wait outside the flock’s route, keep access to water open and keep dogs and vehicles away. If birds stop feeding or repeatedly take flight as you approach, increase the distance. articles.title: Sandwich Tern
articles.body: Sandwich Tern Thalasseus sandvicensis Identity and identification Sandwich Tern Thalasseus sandvicensis belongs to Laridae; older references use Sterna sandvicensis. Adult plumage includes a long black bill with a yellow tip, black legs and a dark crest. The forecrown becomes whiter outside breeding; bill colour alone is insufficient when comparing juveniles. Habitat and food It searches coastal water from the air and plunge-dives for small fish. Beaches, structures and islands provide resting places, preferably near feeding areas. Breeding and development Colonies nest on sandy or shingly ground. BTO gives a typical clutch of one or two eggs, shared incubation of 21–29 days and fledging about 28–30 days after hatching. Parents feed the growing chicks; breeding plumage alone does not establish local nesting. Arab occurrence and seasonality Qatar’s current list calls it a scarce winter visitor, with records in every month. Lebanon’s 2020 checklist explains that records from 2008–2019 support fairly common winter status after earlier assessments of extreme rarity. November suits winter observation without assigning breeding status to either country. Observation and conservation Avoid repeated approaches to resting sites and colonies. Loss of shore habitat and reduced fish resources affect its environment. articles.title: Saudi Falcons and Hunting Exhibition 2026: Al-Melwah, Auctions and Artificial Intelligence
articles.body: A falconer holds a falcon during Al-Melwah race activities at the Saudi Falcons and Hunting Exhibition 2026. The International Saudi Falcons and Hunting Exhibition 2026 in Malham, north of Riyadh, brings together falconry, competitions, auctions, hunting and shooting equipment and modern technologies. This year’s programme goes beyond a conventional exhibition to offer a broad view of hunting, falconry and related activities. Running from 1 to 10 October, the exhibition has seen several noteworthy developments in recent days, led by the start of Al-Melwah racing, Mongolian falcon auctions and the presentation of AI-enhanced technologies for monitoring, tracking and protection. Al-Melwah: 12 Heats and SAR 723,000 in Prizes Al-Melwah racing has begun at the exhibition, with falcons competing to cover 200 metres in the fastest possible time. This year’s edition comprises 12 heats divided between owners and amateurs, and elite and professional competitors. It includes six categories of young falcons: saker, peregrine, pure gyrfalcon, muthallath pure gyrfalcon, gyr-taba and gyr-peregrine. Total prize money reaches SAR 723,000. Participation is restricted to young falcons purchased at the International Falcon Breeders Auction, directly linking the competition to falcon breeding and production. Mongolian Falcons Attract Substantial Bids A falcon presented at the Mongolian falcon auction within the exhibition. Elsewhere at the exhibition, Mongolian falcons have attracted falconers and buyers to their dedicated auction. One auction night saw two falcons sell for a combined SAR 550,000: a young saker for SAR 150,000 and an adult saker for SAR 400,000. On another night, two young saker falcons sold for a total of SAR 350,000, one fetching SAR 250,000 and the other SAR 100,000. Mongolian saker falcons command particular interest among falconers for their size, endurance, long wings and varied plumage, characteristics that contribute to their value in the falcon market. Artificial Intelligence Enters Monitoring and Protection Visitors learn about displays at the Ministry of Interior pavilion. The developments at the exhibition extend beyond falcons and competitions. The Ministry of Interior pavilion presents digital solutions and AI-enhanced technologies used in monitoring, tracking and response, alongside technologies associated with environmental protection and the sustainability of marine resources. The pavilion also introduces visitors to regulations governing the possession and carrying of hunting firearms, as well as rules relating to sea fishing. This technological presence reflects a growing shift in the relationship between hunting and wildlife management, as monitoring, data analysis and tracking become an increasing part of protection and regulation. More Than 5,000 Products Traditional sea-fishing crafts feature in the exhibition’s 2026 edition. The exhibition also features a substantial area dedicated to firearms, ammunition and hunting and shooting equipment, displaying more than 5,000 products representing over 181 international brands. Exhibits include firearms and accessories, optics, equipment and products associated with hunting and outdoor travel. Sea fishing also features in the 2026 programme, with traditional tools and crafts relating to boats, nets and rope-making. This broadens the exhibition to encompass hunting on land and fishing at sea, alongside falconry and shooting. Between Al-Melwah races, auctions recording prices of hundreds of thousands of riyals and the expansion of equipment and modern technologies, the International Saudi Falcons and Hunting Exhibition 2026 offers a comprehensive picture of a sector combining heritage, industry, trade and technology.

articles.title: Sayd Returns… In a New Look and a Wider Vision
articles.body: The harsh circumstances Lebanon has lived through in recent years imposed their challenges on many institutions and sectors, and Sayd’s site was not far from their effects. Today, despite some of those circumstances continuing, the site returns to reclaim its presence and role, and to set out toward a new stage with a wider vision and a renewed look. Sayd returns to take its natural place as a specialized platform in the world of responsible hunting, equestrianism, shooting, and gear, and opens further onto nature, wildlife, ecotourism, and heritage—placing knowledge and responsibility at the heart of its relationship with the hunter, the athlete, and lovers of nature. This return comes with the start of a new season that brings many files worth following: from bird migration and autumn to hunting, its seasons, and its issues; and from equestrianism and shooting to activities and events linked to nature. Sayd will be present to follow them, ask questions about them, and convey experience, information, and image to its audience. Sayd returns… and this is the beginning of a new stage. Editorial Board

articles.title: Short-eared Owl
articles.body: Short-eared Owl Asio flammeus Identity, life and distribution Short-eared Owl Asio flammeus has mottled plumage and yellow eyes surrounded by dark patches. Its small ear tufts can be difficult to see; these are feathers, not the actual ears. It hunts over grassland, marshes and other open ground, sometimes by day. Small mammals are important prey, and food availability influences its movements and breeding success. It nests on the ground. BTO gives a typical clutch of four to seven eggs, but this does not establish local breeding wherever a wintering bird is seen. Leave resting birds a wide buffer. A 2016 OSME-published study describes it as a very rare winter visitor and probable very rare passage migrant in Lebanon. Its scarcity there does not establish equal scarcity elsewhere, and the photograph, taken in the United States, does not document a Lebanese observation. www.bto.org — Short-eared Owl · www.rspb.org.uk — Short-eared Owl · osme.org — Short-eared Owl Photo: Chrissy McClarren and Andy Reago

articles.title: The shrike: a bird that executes its prey on thorns
articles.body: A small bird turns thorns into tools for holding prey and storing food. How does it do it, and where can shrikes be seen in Arab countries? A thorny branch, an impaled mouse, and a small bird with a black mask standing nearby. The scene resembles a gallows in the wild, yet its maker needs neither an eagle’s bulk nor a falcon’s talons. This is the shrike, a bird that turns a thorn into a tool for securing its prey and a dining table. It may make the branches of a single shrub into a store of meals to return to later. From a distance, it looks like an unassuming grey bird on a high branch. But that perch is a lookout. Its eyes follow movement on the ground, its hooked bill ready to strike at a large insect, a lizard or a small rodent. Once the prey is in its hands—or rather, between its bill and its feet—the thorns enter the story. The thorn that stands in for a talon The shrike belongs to the passerines, but lives as a predator. Without the powerful talons of birds of prey, it uses what its surroundings provide: a sharp thorn, barbed wire or a crevice between two branches. It secures its prey, then uses its bill to tear off pieces to eat. The thorn becomes an extension of its natural equipment: it holds what is difficult to grip and helps the bird handle prey large in relation to its own size. Part of the prey may remain for another meal, or surplus catches may be impaled rather than eaten straight away. This harsh-looking spectacle therefore serves several purposes: controlling food, making it easier to eat and keeping it for later. Insects and small vertebrates on branches within a shrike’s territory can look like an open record of its hunting success. When a food store becomes an advertisement Another detail makes the story more remarkable. In a study of Great Grey Shrikes in Poland, researchers found that males selected more conspicuous places to impale prey during the mating season. This suggests that their stores may also serve a social purpose: food that can be seen may carry a message to a potential mate or a rival. It is an ingenious use of space. A shrub provides a lookout, a tool for securing prey, a food store and, sometimes, a display stand. Among the shrikes that practise this behaviour, the Great Grey Shrike occurs across substantial parts of the Arab world. Some populations are resident in particular countries; others arrive on migration or in winter. Identification Arabic name: الصرد الرمادي الكبير. English name: Great Grey Shrike. French name: Pie-grièche grise. Scientific name: Lanius excubitor. Family: Laniidae. Order: Passeriformes. Length: about 24–25 centimetres. Weight: around 48–81 grams according to The Birds of Saudi Arabia, with variation among populations. Key features: a grey back, a black mask through the eye, a long tail, black-and-white wings, and a bill with a hooked tip. Food: large insects, lizards, rodents and small birds. Global status: Least Concern, according to the global assessment cited in the references. This does not mean that its numbers cannot decline or that all its populations are equally abundant. Where can it be seen in Arab countries? — The Maghreb Local resident populations live in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, in northern habitats as well as deserts and oases. Libya also has resident populations. In suitable habitats, shrikes can therefore be encountered throughout the year, not only during a short passage season. Their plumage varies in shades of grey and white. Some older references placed these birds under Southern Grey Shrike, but their classification has since changed. This article follows AviList 2026, which includes the relevant North African and Arabian populations, as well as Steppe Grey Shrike, within Great Grey Shrike Lanius excubitor. Egypt Resident breeding populations are documented, including at Gebel Elba and in the Red Sea mountains. In the Western Desert, shrikes have been recorded securing prey on boxthorn spines and barbed wire. The striking ‘gallows’ scene is not remote from our own landscapes. Saudi Arabia and the Gulf In Saudi Arabia, the Great Grey Shrike is a widespread resident breeder, with additional passage and wintering populations. The Birds of Saudi Arabia describes its use of acacia thorns to impale prey in the central and western parts of the country. The United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Oman have resident breeding Arabian populations, joined by Steppe Grey Shrikes on passage or in winter. In the UAE specifically, autumn passage generally extends from August to October and spring passage from March to April, with some birds remaining over winter. Resident birds can be seen throughout the year. Kuwait is different: its checklist treats Steppe Grey Shrike as an uncommon passage migrant and winter visitor, while the Arabian population resident in neighbouring countries is a vagrant. There is no single calendar of occurrence for the entire Gulf. The Levant In Jordan, Great Grey Shrike is listed as resident. Its status in Syria varies with population and region, from rare local breeding to winter visits and passage. For Lebanon, the checklist published in 2020 records historical breeding, but found no conclusive recent evidence of it at the time of preparation. It documents scarce or rare passage in October to mid-November, and very rare passage from early March to early April. The bird should therefore not be presented as a common resident in Lebanon today. Where to look in the field Look for open country with scattered shrubs or trees: farmland, the edges of oases, semi-desert, or places with thorny vegetation and perches overlooking the ground. The first thing you notice is often its exposed position on a branch or wire, followed by the black mask and long tail. It can resemble other grey shrikes. A clear photograph of the head, wings and tail, together with the location and date, helps identification. Differences in colour do not necessarily indicate a different species: age and local population also play a part. Nest and family The shrike builds a cup-shaped nest in a tree or shrub, using twigs, grasses and rootlets, and lining it with softer material. The female does most of the incubation, and both parents care for the young. Saudi and Emirati references usually report 3–4 eggs, sometimes more. Incubation lasts about 15–17 days, and the young leave the nest after roughly two and a half weeks. Breeding timing varies geographically: March to May is prominent in the UAE, though activity may begin earlier. Scattered shrubs and trees remain an important part of its habitat. Photographers and birdwatchers should leave impaled prey where it is, keep away from nests and avoid rearranging a scene for a picture. You may leave while the mouse remains on its thorn. To a passer-by, it is a startling image; to the shrike, it is part of a way of life in which a small branch becomes a tool that gives it power beyond its size. articles.title: From Sicily to Lebanon: The Battle to Save Migratory Birds from Illegal Hunting
articles.body: European Turtle Doves in Douz, Tunisia.Photo: Skander Zarrad. As autumn migration continues, efforts to protect birds are unfolding on several fronts around the Mediterranean: legal action in Sicily, the seizure of nets in Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, a defence of field cooperation in Cyprus, and warnings about large hunting hauls in Libya. These different events share a common aim: safeguarding birds’ journeys between their breeding grounds and wintering areas. Sicily: A Court Halts Early Hunting of Turtle Doves In Sicily, nature conservation organisations have secured a legal advance for the European Turtle Dove. According to a statement published by LEAL on 4 September, the region’s Council of Administrative Justice upheld the suspension of hunting this species during the early opening of the season, following legal action led by LEAL and Pro Natura, with support from the Committee Against Bird Slaughter (CABS) and Green Impact. The decision concerns the early hunting of turtle doves specifically; it does not amount to a ban on all hunting on the island. Its significance lies in reducing pressure on the species at a sensitive stage of its seasonal journey. Lebanon: More Than 20,000 Square Metres of Nets In Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, the Internal Security Forces announced the seizure of illegal hunting nets covering a total area of 20,640 square metres, during a campaign carried out by the Bekaa Investigation Detachment of the Regional Gendarmerie Unit. The campaign coincides with the autumn bird protection camp run in Lebanon by CABS in cooperation with the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching (MECSHAP), amid daily field cooperation between the organisations participating in the camp and the security forces. CABS announced the launch of the camp on 8 September, despite tense regional conditions, to monitor migration routes and combat the trapping of birds with nets and limesticks. Hunting nets and poles seized during the security forces’ campaign in the Bekaa Valley. Cyprus: Defending Cooperation with the Authorities In Cyprus, the debate has reached parliament. Ahead of a meeting of the parliamentary environment committee in mid-September, CABS urged lawmakers to protect cooperation between civil society organisations, the police and the authorities responsible for combating illegal hunting, warning of attempts to disrupt it. The case shows that bird protection depends not only on fieldwork, but also on maintaining the institutional framework that enables violations to be detected and pursued. Libya: When Hunting Hauls Become a Competition On the African shore, Libya’s Al-Barari nature conservation organisation warned about circulating photographs of large hauls of European Turtle Doves. According to a report by Al-Wasat, the organisation said one of the photographs showed more than 700 birds. The organisation warned that displaying such hauls could turn into a competition that encourages further hunting, and called for the circumstances and legality of the hunting to be investigated. It also raised concerns about trade in the birds — a matter that requires investigation and cannot be established by photographs alone. A flock of migrating White Storks over Istanbul.Photo: Tema. Protection Beyond Borders The events, organisations and methods differ, but the issue extends beyond any one country. Birds travel along interconnected routes, and protection at one stop on their journey remains incomplete if nets or illegal hunting await them elsewhere. From courtrooms to field patrols, complementary forms of protection help safeguard migration and conserve nature. articles.title: Widespread environmental destruction in southern Lebanon threatens one of the world’s key bird-migration flyways
articles.body: Thick white smoke over vegetation in the south — documentation linked to the use of white phosphorus munitions, according to reports by international organizations. Since October 2023, and through the escalation of March 2026, southern Lebanon has continued to see documented environmental destruction, recorded by several international and local bodies, that has hit forests, farmland, soil, and water. To this day (September 2026), and despite Lebanon and Israel signing a US-sponsored framework agreement on 26 June 2026, Israeli raids and explosions continue in southern border areas. White phosphorus: international documentation Human Rights Watch documented the Israeli army’s use of white phosphorus munitions in at least 17 towns in southern Lebanon. According to data gathered by the Lebanese researcher Ahmad Baydoun with the group “Al-Janoubiyyun al-Khudr” (the Southern Greens), more than 918 hectares were damaged in 191 documented white-phosphorus attacks between October 2023 and the ceasefire in November 2024. Amnesty International documented that Israel began using white phosphorus in Lebanon between 10 and 16 October 2023. Its use in populated areas violates Protocol III of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons. On the scientific side, the Lebanese National Council for Scientific Research estimated that at least 2,000 hectares of forest, olive and citrus groves, and farmland were partly destroyed by white phosphorus. Among the losses, the historic woodland “Horj al-Rahib” was destroyed — a 16-hectare oak forest on the edge of Aita al-Shaab. The Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS), in a detailed report, also recorded Israel’s use of white phosphorus munitions that set wide fires in farmland, killing vegetation and causing long-term degradation of soil and water. Fires consuming vegetation on a rocky hill near inhabited areas in southern Lebanon Migratory birds in the line of fire Lebanon lies on one of the world’s most important bird-migration corridors. It forms the second most important migration route for birds between Europe, the Middle East, Asia, and Africa, also known as the African–Eurasian flyway or the Eastern Mediterranean flyway. Millions of birds of more than 400 species cross it, between breeding sites in central and eastern Europe and wintering grounds in central and eastern Africa, among them the White Stork, the Lesser Spotted Eagle, and pelicans. A specialist study published in 2026 in the journal Environment and Security concluded that drone warfare generates “multi-layered environmental risks,” among them noise disturbance, pollution from electronic debris, and behavioural stress in wildlife, especially birds. The study indicates that birds may interpret the sound of drones as an aerial predator, which can drive panicked flight, disrupt feeding, or cause them to abandon nest sites. More serious still, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) confirmed in its 2025 assessment the global extinction of the Slender-billed Curlew (Numenius tenuirostris), one of the first officially recorded extinctions of a migratory bird species. This bird was among the species that relied specifically on the southern Lebanon corridor within their migration route. The IUCN warns that migratory birds already face accumulated pressures from habitat loss, urban expansion, pesticides, and climate change, in addition to the reality of conflict zones damaged by white-phosphorus pollution and heavy metals. In October 2025, during the IUCN World Conservation Congress in Abu Dhabi, members adopted a resolution calling for the rehabilitation of Lebanon’s damaged ecosystems, recognising wide environmental degradation that includes soil and water pollution, loss of vegetation cover, erosion, fire risk, and the threat to ecological connectivity between habitats.

articles.title: Stock Dove
articles.body: Stock Dove Columba oenas Identity, life and distribution Stock Dove Columba oenas is a blue-grey pigeon with an iridescent green neck patch. Its Arabic common name is a broad everyday expression for wild pigeon, making the scientific name especially important for precision. It lacks the Woodpigeon’s white neck patch and shows short black wing bars. Separating it from Rock Dove and domestic forms requires several characters rather than grey colour alone. Its habitat combines farmland for feeding with large, cavity-bearing trees for nesting. BTO reports a typical clutch of two eggs. Losing old trees can therefore remove nest sites even when feeding fields remain available. Occurrence beside farmland does not make it a feral domestic pigeon. Useful documentation combines wing and neck views with locality, without chasing the bird. The accompanying photograph is illustrative, not evidence of local breeding. The African Bird Club documents the species in Morocco. This alone does not provide a detailed seasonal map for Arab countries or establish resident breeding wherever it is observed. www.bto.org — Stock Dove · www.rspb.org.uk — Stock Dove · www.africanbirdclub.org — Stock Dove Photo: Cristina Hutchison

articles.title: Tree Pipit
articles.body: Tree Pipit Anthus trivialis Identity and names Tree Pipit, Pipit des arbres in French, is Anthus trivialis, a small migrant in Motacillidae, the pipit and wagtail family, and the order Passeriformes. It is about 15 cm long. Despite its tree-associated name, it spends considerable time feeding on the ground. It needs a mixture of open ground, grassy vegetation and scattered trees rather than only dense, closed woodland with little light reaching the floor. Identification The brown, olive-tinged upperparts are streaked. The warm-coloured breast has conspicuous dark streaks, finer streaking continues along the flanks, and the belly is relatively white. It resembles Meadow Pipit, but has a heavier bill, a shorter, more curved hind claw and clearer breast-to-belly contrast. The claw is difficult to assess at a distance, and perching on a branch does not establish identity. Males and females look similar; assigning sex or age from one photograph requires caution. A natural flight call, combined with clear views of face, breast and flank, is more useful than colour intensity alone. Habitat, food and behaviour It uses woodland edges, clearings, pasture and cultivated land during migration, sometimes also gardens or pond margins where food and cover are available. It picks insects and small invertebrates from the ground and low vegetation, walking quietly through them. During breeding, the male is known for a song-flight that rises from a perch and descends gradually like a parachute. That behaviour belongs to a breeding context: a silent bird crossing an Arab agricultural landscape may be engaged in a very different activity. Recording habitat and feeding behaviour adds useful information to a species name and photograph. Range and Arab occurrence It breeds across large parts of Europe and Asia, with populations moving to Africa and southern Asia outside the breeding season. Lebanon’s 2026 guide describes common passage from March to early May and from late August to late November, peaking in September–October. Early-December and late-February records may represent passage rather than winter residence. In Kuwait it is a common passage migrant and scarce winter visitor, recorded in agricultural areas including Al Abraq and Jahra. Oman’s official list describes it as common on passage and in winter. These examples show that seasonal status changes between countries and cannot be inferred from a general range map alone. Breeding and development The nest is on the ground, concealed among vegetation, not high in the tree from which the male sings. BTO gives a typical clutch of 4–5 eggs, incubated by the female for about 13 days, and a nestling period of about 12.5–13.5 days. Young chicks require feeding in the nest. Leaving it does not mean instant independence, and British laying dates should not be applied throughout the global range. Breeding conditions vary, and passage through an Arab farm does not demonstrate nesting there. November and responsible observation November can remain part of autumn passage in Lebanon while overlapping documented winter occurrence in Oman and Kuwait at different levels of abundance. Observe from a permitted field edge or path and wait rather than following birds through vegetation. Record streaking and any naturally given calls without using playback to draw birds closer. Include numbers, vegetation, behaviour and observation time, and retain a tentative identification if distinguishing features remain unclear. Avoiding private land and possible nest sites protects both birds and relationships with landowners. Conservation The global IUCN category is Least Concern (LC), which does not negate regional declines or local pressures. The Lebanon guide identifies agricultural intensification, habitat loss and deterioration, illegal hunting and climate change; the Kuwaiti reference also identifies habitat loss and degradation. Protecting grassy margins, clearings and scattered trees, while reducing pesticide impacts, helps maintain food and shelter. Conserving a bird called Tree Pipit does not mean planting dense trees everywhere: the mixture of open vegetation and perches is central to understanding its needs. articles.title: Tufted Duck
articles.body: Tufted Duck Aythya fuligula — a diving duck on passage and wintering waters Identity and names The Tufted Duck is a diving waterbird in the family Anatidae and order Anseriformes, scientifically named Aythya fuligula. Arabic references use “Batta Qanbaraa”; Saudi and Libyan sources also record “Abu Khusla”, while the Kuwait checklist uses “al-Hadhaf al-Muqanza”. These are documented names for the same species, not separate species. Calling it a diving duck describes its feeding method; it does not place it in the grebe family. Recognising males, females and young An adult male contrasts black head, breast and back with white flanks. A tuft hangs behind the head, which can show a purple sheen depending on the light. The eye is yellow and the bill blue-grey with a broad black tip. Females are predominantly dark brown, with paler flanks and a much shorter tuft; a variable white patch may surround the bill base. The face pattern alone therefore cannot establish identification. Young birds appear duller and may retain narrow, brown juvenile wing feathers into their first winter, unlike adult feathers; ageing at a distance is not always reliable. Males also become less contrasting in post-breeding eclipse plumage. Both sexes show a conspicuous white wing bar in flight. Male Greater Scaup Aythya marila have grey rather than black backs. Females require comparison of tuft, head shape, back colour and bill pattern together, rather than expecting an obvious tuft on every bird. Habitat, diet and behaviour It uses lakes, ponds and reservoirs, including artificial waterbodies, and sometimes sheltered coastal waters. Open swimming water matters, but does not remove its need for suitable margins for resting or nesting. It dives for molluscs and aquatic invertebrates and also eats seeds and plant material: it is neither exclusively carnivorous nor exclusively vegetarian. It may join other ducks and spend long periods resting or sleeping on the water. A quiet flock does not mean a site is unused for feeding: a brief visit cannot reveal its full activity cycle. Recording numbers, behaviour and water conditions is more informative than recording the species name alone. Distribution and Arab-country occurrence It breeds across large parts of Eurasia, and migrant populations winter south of their northern breeding range. Movements are not identical everywhere: parts of Britain have resident birds whose numbers increase with winter arrivals, illustrating why one country’s status should not be transferred to another. In Saudi Arabia it is primarily a winter visitor during October–February and a rare passage migrant; the Saudi reference does not report breeding in the kingdom. Some individuals may remain through summer without proving nesting. Kuwait’s official list classifies it as a rare passage migrant and winter visitor. The Oman field guide lists it as a winter visitor, while UAE reports document winter occurrence, particularly on certain lakes. In Lebanon it is an uncommon passage migrant in Beqaa wetlands from mid-September to late November, with a few remaining in winter. Libya’s wintering-waterbird atlas documented limited occurrence during its 2005–2010 surveys; these represent a defined study period, not a current census. AEWA also records occurrence in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Egypt and Iraq, but national listing alone does not establish abundance or the season at every site. Breeding and life cycle The nest is made of vegetation near water, sometimes on an island or among grasses. A female typically lays 8–11 eggs and incubates for about 25 days. Chicks hatch downy and mobile and usually become capable of flight at around 45–50 days. These are typical durations rather than a fixed schedule for every nest. They should not be presented as an Arab breeding calendar: the regional occurrence described here is predominantly passage and winter presence. Late October and conservation Late October overlaps autumn passage in Lebanon and the winter occurrence window reported for Saudi Arabia. It is therefore a useful moment to learn the species, without claiming simultaneous arrival throughout the Arab world. Its global category in the 2025 assessment is Least Concern (LC), with an overall decreasing population trend; the category does not mean an absence of pressures. Risks include wetland degradation, pollution, disturbance and hunting. Practical protection depends on suitable water and quiet resting areas. Watch from a distance that does not cause escape, and never chase birds to reveal their tuft or wing bar. articles.title: Tracking turtle-doves from Azerbaijan to the Nile exposes a difficult migration route
articles.body: GPS data reveal sea and desert crossings, critical stopovers and substantial gaps in knowledge. Perlman et al. / Bird Conservation International (CC BY 4.0) A migratory route is more than a line across a map. For the European Turtle-dove (Streptopelia turtur), it is a chain of habitats where birds must find food and rest while crossing seas, deserts and human-altered landscapes. A peer-reviewed study published online in Bird Conservation International on 8 October 2026 describes GPS tracking of 26 turtle-doves tagged in Azerbaijan and the eastern Mediterranean. Sixteen were recorded beginning southward migration; two provided particularly extensive tracks reaching Sudan and South Sudan. During active migration, the tracked turtle-doves covered up to 752 kilometres in a day. Among birds with sufficiently detailed tracking data, the longest measured continuous flight covered 719 kilometres in 13 hours. Their routes included crossings of the Red Sea and desert. Farmland along the Nile emerged as an important stopover environment, particularly in Egypt and Sudan. The conservation implication is regional: protecting breeding grounds cannot substitute for maintaining stopover habitats along an entire flyway. Hunting pressure and habitat change must be considered across borders. These tracks are not a definitive map for the species. The sample is limited and most tagged birds did not yield complete migration records. The researchers therefore identify promising areas for further study rather than claiming comprehensive coverage. articles.title: Vultures talk before they hatch
articles.body: From egg to nest: photographs of recording work in the Netherlands during the 2024–2025 study period. Soft calls from inside the egg reveal the beginnings of a rich vocal world in Rüppell’s vultures—and could open a new avenue for conservation. The sound comes first, from inside the egg; the chick’s arrival follows. That is how the story begins for Rüppell’s vultures, whose vocal lives appear far richer than their supposedly silent image suggests. Researchers documented soft calls produced before hatching in a study published in PLOS One on 21 October 2026. According to Utrecht University, the chicks begin making these sounds about two days before they emerge. Original recording of a Rüppell’s vulture egg before hatching Download recording Video S2 from the study’s supplementary material, approximately 18 seconds. Increase the volume or use headphones for this quiet recording. A single call from inside the egg Download recording Audio S1 is a very short sample of one call from inside the egg, lasting approximately 0.22 seconds. A voice before emergence The study describes soft, tonal calls beginning after the chick breaks into the egg’s air chamber and starts breathing with its lungs. The calls continue through hatching and appear to develop into the chick’s post-hatching sounds, becoming more variable. Artificial incubation at Rotterdam’s Diergaarde Blijdorp offered an opportunity to record this stage. Whether parents answer their chick’s calls while it is still inside the egg could not be determined by the study. A society with calls of its own The team, led by Connor Proudfoot, studied two groups of Rüppell’s vultures in the Netherlands, comprising 35 birds, and analysed 2,500 calls. Recordings collected between September 2024 and May 2025 covered feeding, competition, reproduction and care of young. The researchers distinguished 16 call types: some clearly differentiated, others graded and overlapping. This vocal world includes food-begging calls, calls associated with resource defence or receiving aggression, and sounds accompanying the feeding of chicks. Its diversity offers a window into the social life of a bird often described as quiet. Could sound help conserve the species? Rüppell’s vulture, Gyps rueppelli, is critically endangered. The significance of the research therefore extends beyond the surprising sound inside an egg to a practical question: could hearing these calls help parents prepare for their chick’s arrival? In artificial-incubation programmes, a model may replace the real egg, and chicks return to the nest only several days after hatching. The researchers propose testing the role of pre-hatching calls and their potential future use in improving chick acceptance and breeding success. This remains a proposed research step; the study has not tested that effect. The beginning of a fuller picture The study provides a quantitative description of the species’ vocal repertoire, rather than the final word on it. The work took place in captivity: wild populations may use calls or encounter contexts not represented in the recordings, including interactions during soaring flight. Behind the silent bird of popular imagination is a world worth listening to. Photographs: Connor Proudfoot; recordings: Proudfoot et al. © 2026 Proudfoot et al. articles.title: Water Pipit
articles.body: Water Pipit Anthus spinoletta Identity and identification Water Pipit Anthus spinoletta belongs to Motacillidae. Winter plumage shows a pale eyebrow, streaked breast and usually dark legs. The breeding breast becomes less streaked and pinkish. Compare face, wings and legs with Meadow Pipit: a photograph beside water cannot establish identity by itself. Habitat and food It collects insects and other invertebrates from damp ground and water margins. Populations breed in mountain grasslands, moving to lower, warmer habitats outside breeding. Breeding and development The ground nest is concealed among vegetation. BTO gives a typical clutch of 4–5 eggs, female incubation of 14–15 days and nest departure around 15–16 days. Hatchlings cannot support themselves and need feeding; nest departure is not full independence. Arab occurrence and seasonality Lebanon’s 2020 checklist describes widespread passage from mid-September to late November and mid-February to early May, with scarce, local wintering in wetlands. Qatar’s current list classifies it as a common winter visitor. November thus connects Lebanese passage with Qatar’s winter season, at different abundance. Observation and conservation Retaining wet margins and damp grassland preserves feeding habitat. Watch without repeatedly displacing birds between feeding patches. articles.title: When the coast changes… where do birds rest?
articles.body: Batroun’s pelican at the edge of the Mediterranean. Amira Rajab / dpa The Lebanon–Cyprus–Egypt triangle: estuaries, salt pans, lakes and harbours in the protection of bird habitats. In 2026, reports on managing Lebanon’s Damour basin, a new study of Egypt’s Lake Manzala and the debate over expanding Latchi harbour in Cyprus reopen one question: where do birds rest when the coast changes? At the water’s edge, they need an estuary that still receives river water, a shallow bank rich in food, sheltering reeds or a quiet rock after diving. These features make a place valuable as habitat and deserve a place in development plans from the outset. Lebanon | From the Damour estuary to Anfeh’s salt pans Anfeh’s salt pans beside the Mediterranean. EPA / The National In 2026, the integrated management plan for Damour brings the relationship between river and coast back into focus. Reports reveal the pressures on the area: around 200.7 hectares of agricultural land were converted to built-up uses between 2014 and 2024 within the basin study area, alongside water abstraction, pollution and construction along riverbanks. These pressures are particularly important at the estuary and its surroundings, where freshwater meets the sea and the river connects with farmland and coastal vegetation. This area provides habitat for migratory birds in Lebanon. Surveys of the lower Damour have recorded migratory and resident species, including White Pelican and Common Crane. Protecting the estuary therefore means preserving a space used by birds and its connections with water and surrounding vegetation. Recent reports identify the flow of water reaching the estuary as a management priority, alongside restoring riverbanks and regulating land use. Protecting the coast is tied to what happens upstream: abstraction, pollution and encroachment have consequences along the river all the way to the sea. On the northern coast, Anfeh’s salt pans reveal another aspect of this relationship. Between sea and rock lie shallow basins created by the craft of salt harvesting, bringing together work, heritage and nature. Sources document their role as resting and feeding sites for migratory birds, while some abandoned pools have become refuges. Areas that may appear unused thus retain a living function along birds’ journeys. The salt pans face pressure from changes in coastal land use and tourism development, making their protection about more than preserving a traditional occupation. Safeguarding the basins, their connection to the sea and their open character can allow salt production to continue while retaining feeding and resting sites for birds. On Batroun’s beach, the famous ‘Bajou3a’ gives the relationship between birds and the coast a familiar face. Her image beside the sea brings the question closer to people: where do birds find rest and food, and how can we preserve these spaces as the shoreline changes? Egypt | Manzala: more open water… different habitats A wader at the water’s edge in Port Said. اليوم السابع A scientific study published in 2026 places Lake Manzala before a precise question: how does bird life change when open water expands at the expense of reeds and shallow margins? The study compared twenty sites within Ashtoum El Gamil Protectorate, in the lake’s north-eastern area, before and after dredging and vegetation removal. It found declines in vegetation cover, bird diversity and abundance within the study area, with different responses among bird groups depending on the habitats they use. A wader searches for food in shallow water and mud, while other birds benefit from open water. When water depth changes or vegetation disappears, the opportunities available to each group change too. A lake can therefore appear larger and more open while losing some of the habitats that give it its diversity. The study recommends allowing reeds to recolonise and restoring shallow, muddy areas along the margins. These recommendations connect lake rehabilitation with birds’ needs: open water for diving and swimming, vegetation for shelter and nesting, and banks for feeding and resting. This diversity is especially important at Ashtoum El Gamil, where the lake environment meets the Mediterranean. Differences in water, vegetation and margins create a series of habitats that birds use in different ways. Successful rehabilitation is also measured by the diversity a place retains. Cleaning water and improving circulation can go hand in hand with protecting reeds, shallow areas and islands. When these elements remain, the lake can accommodate birds with varied needs and retain its role as a living coastal environment. Cyprus | Latchi: the harbour on the birds’ map Latchi harbour at the centre of the debate over expansion and protection of the bay. BirdLife Cyprus In October 2026, BirdLife Cyprus renewed the debate over the limits of development through the proposed expansion of Latchi harbour in the island’s north-west. The organisation said the proposal would increase recreational boat capacity from 200 to 384 in Chrysochous Bay, which is surrounded by protected areas and supports seabirds, turtles and the Mediterranean monk seal, alongside Posidonia seagrass meadows. The new element in the debate is what birds’ movements reveal. According to the organisation, data from the Pandoteira project show regular use of the Akamas coast and the bay by the Mediterranean subspecies of European Shag, with young birds frequently visiting the harbour’s surroundings. A space for mooring and navigation on an engineering plan appears on a bird’s map as a place to feed and rest. Tracking devices help explain this relationship: they reveal where birds travel after leaving their nests and which parts of the coast they use during the day. Shags nesting on rocks and coastal islets also need waters in which to find food and places to perch quietly after diving. The organisation warns of increased noise, lighting, pollution and human presence as boat numbers rise, and calls for assessment of cumulative effects across the whole bay. Marine habitats are interconnected, and birds’ movements extend beyond the project boundaries drawn on paper. The significance of the Cypriot case lies in bringing feeding and resting sites into the expansion decision and its conditions, and considering the harbour within its wider environment. Knowing where the nest is does not suffice; the protection map must accommodate the bird’s daily life. What remains at the water’s edge? From Damour and Anfeh to Manzala and Latchi, interventions and birds differ, but the question remains: what do we preserve for them when the coast changes? An estuary that receives water, quiet rocks, reeds and shallow banks deserve to appear in development plans alongside quays and roads. A coast that makes room for people’s lives can also leave birds a place to rest.

articles.title: Where Do Birds Rest?
articles.body: Flamingos at Ras Al Khor against Dubai’s skyline: a bird refuge beside the city. WWF Major migration refuges in the Mashreq and Arabian Peninsula The greater spotted eagle has returned to Kuwait’s Jahra Reserve with the autumn migration season of 2026. Its arrival signals more than the start of a season: a bird travelling long distances has found water, food and somewhere to spend the winter. From Jahra to the wetlands of the Bekaa, Iraq’s marshes and the Arabian coast, these places help make migration possible. World Migratory Bird Day highlights this journey and its need for safe habitats. From the Mashreq to the Arabian Peninsula, we explore some of the major refuges: some provide brief stops to replenish energy; others accommodate birds for months. Routes vary between species: shorebirds need productive shores, ducks suitable waters, and raptors areas offering prey and quiet. Kuwait | Jahra: winter among water and reeds The Kuwait Environment Protection Society’s bird team recorded the first greater spotted eagle at Jahra Reserve this season. This raptor uses wetlands during winter, benefiting from food and resting places. Jahra combines shallow waters, reeds and open ground, attracting birds of different sizes and feeding habits. Its value extends beyond the sight of a rare bird: it illustrates the need for a complete habitat usable throughout the season, supported by continued monitoring and protection. Lebanon | Aammiq: a pause in the Bekaa A glossy ibis forages in shallow water at Aammiq wetlands. Reuters — Ali Hashisho In the Bekaa Valley, Aammiq provides migrating birds with water, reeds and meadows within a broad agricultural landscape. Lebanon’s largest natural freshwater wetland is an important site for passage, feeding and roosting. Ducks, herons and other waterbirds find different resources within this diversity, while other birds use the surrounding land. The glossy ibis, searching shallow water with its curved bill, illustrates the relationship between bird and habitat. Protecting this refuge means caring for water, vegetation and surrounding farmland, and preventing poaching and disturbance at gathering sites. Jordan | Azraq and Aqaba: an oasis and a seaside stop A bluethroat at Azraq: part of the bird diversity associated with the oasis and its surroundings. Birdingplaces Azraq Oasis, in the eastern desert, attracts birds seeking water. Its pools and vegetation offer waterbirds and passing migrants opportunities to feed and rest; maintaining water is central to its ecological role. Further south, Aqaba Bird Observatory provides another stop where desert meets sea. An agreement between the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature and UNDP at the start of October supports the sustainability of its habitats. Together, the two sites illustrate natural habitat protection and restoration in a region where every wetland matters. Syria | Jabbul: refuge in shallow waters East of Aleppo, Sabkhat al-Jabbul is one of Syria’s major wetlands. The shallow saline lake, its margins and islands provide waterbirds with places for passage and wintering, including flamingos and duck species. Different depths and margins allow birds to stand, forage and find quiet. Protecting Jabbul therefore requires maintaining its water and ecological characteristics, together with the surrounding areas used by birds. Iraq | The marshes: reeds and open water In southern Iraq, Hawizeh, Hammar and the Central Marshes offer extensive reeds, open water and shallow wetlands. They form an important part of the network used by waterbirds during migration and winter. This diversity provides feeding, shelter and roosting sites for ducks and other waterbirds. Marsh life depends on water flows and quality, and on surrounding communities. Protection involves managing resources, responsible hunting, and preserving the extent and connections of wetland habitats. Saudi Arabia | Farasan: stops on the Red Sea Pelicans over the waters of Farasan, where shores meet mangroves. Saudi Press Agency (SPA) Off Jazan, the Farasan Islands combine mangroves, sandy and muddy shores, and coastal salt flats. These habitats offer waterbirds and shorebirds several places to feed and rest along the Red Sea routes they use. Winter counts demonstrate the importance of field monitoring. Birds seen above the coast also depend on food in mud and shallow water, and on quiet shores. Protecting Farasan means preserving these details, from mangroves to gathering and roosting areas. Oman | Barr al Hikman: a table revealed by the tide Shorebirds at Barr al Hikman, where shallow water and falling tides reveal feeding areas. Times of Oman In Al Wusta Governorate, Barr al Hikman’s mudflats extend along coasts rich in life. Receding tides reveal broad feeding areas, making the site a major winter refuge for shorebirds in the region. These birds depend on the tidal cycle: they feed on exposed mud and gather on higher ground as water rises. Feeding areas and nearby resting sites therefore need protection together. Disturbance that repeatedly forces flocks into flight consumes energy needed for their stay and onward journey. United Arab Emirates | Ras Al Khor: refuge beside the city In Dubai, Ras Al Khor offers a striking view of birds against the city. Its wetlands and shallow waters host flamingos feeding on small organisms in habitat providing food and rest. Ras Al Khor illustrates the importance of retaining space for nature within cities. Water alone is insufficient: birds need healthy habitat, quiet areas and managed viewing that allows visitors to enjoy the flocks without disturbing them. Every observation helps These sites are examples within a wider network supporting migration. This year’s occasion stresses the importance of every bird and observation. Birdwatchers, photographers and responsible hunters can contribute by recording species, location and date, keeping their distance and reporting violations. Protecting the journey begins with knowing where birds stop, then keeping those places safe.

articles.title: Whinchat
articles.body: Whinchat Saxicola rubetra — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and recognition The Whinchat, Saxicola rubetra, is a small member of the flycatcher family Muscicapidae. Its Arabic names include al-qulay‘i and al-birqish al-ahmar. Males show a clear white eyebrow above dark cheeks, with an orange throat and breast. Females are less contrasting, with browner cheeks and an eyebrow paler than the surrounding feathers. The back is brown and streaked; the relatively short tail has white at the sides of its base. Juveniles are more conspicuously spotted or mottled, so not every dull bird is an adult female. Distinguishing similar birds European and Siberian Stonechats are the main identification challenges. Combine the prominent eyebrow, streaked brown rump and white sides to the tail base, together with the longer primary projection beyond the inner feathers of the folded wing. A white patch may show on the wing coverts, but can be very reduced in first-autumn birds: its absence does not exclude Whinchat. Autumn identification should therefore compare head, rump and tail rather than rely on orange colouring shared with other chats. Habitat, food and behaviour Meadows, grassland and pasture provide habitat where tall stems or scattered bushes offer lookout posts. Fields and cultivated areas are also visited on migration. From a stem, fence or low shrub, the bird watches before darting after prey on the ground or in the air. Insects and other invertebrates dominate the diet, with some fruits and seeds taken in autumn. Dense woodland is less important than prey-rich open ground with appropriately spaced perches. Breeding and annual cycle The breeding range extends across Europe to western Siberia. The low nest is concealed among grasses or at the base of vegetation, making early mowing and grassland disturbance important risks. Accounts commonly describe four to seven eggs. The female incubates for approximately two weeks, and young leave the nest after roughly another fortnight, before they are fully independent. Dates vary regionally; a bird seen in an Arab field during autumn is not evidence that it nests there. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Wintering is mainly in tropical Africa, with Arab countries providing migration routes and stopping places. Jordan’s checklist and Qatar e-Nature classify it as a passage migrant; Qatar Bird Observation Group places passage mainly in April–May and September–October. Saudi Arabia’s Birds of AlUla guide records a scarce migrant at Harrat Khaybar within the guide’s local survey area. Kuwaiti references describe uncommon passage and rare winter visits. The global distribution account also confirms occurrence in Egypt and Maghreb countries. October sightings must therefore be interpreted locally, rather than automatically labelled the arrival of a regular winter resident. Ecology and conservation Whinchats connect grassland invertebrates with higher predators. European monitoring highlights grassland deterioration, agricultural intensification and poor breeding success; protecting nesting cover from early mowing is particularly relevant. Migrants also require stopping places with food and shelter. The global category is Least Concern, but documented declines in individual countries remain important. Monitoring Arab-region populations remains important for establishing their own trends. articles.title: Whiskered Tern
articles.body: Whiskered Tern Chlidonias hybrida Identity and names Whiskered Tern, Guifette moustac in French, is Chlidonias hybrida, a species in Laridae and the order Charadriiformes. Arabic names include al-kharshana al-sablaa and the Lebanon guide’s “hybrid tern”. It is a small marsh tern, approximately 24–28 cm long depending on the reference. The word “hybrid” in a vernacular name does not mean an individual produced by two different species: this is a recognised species. Its relatively stocky body and short, shallowly forked tail distinguish it from many marine terns. Identification Breeding plumage combines a black cap and white cheeks with a grey body and darker belly; bill and legs are dark red. Outside breeding, the underparts and forehead become white and the crown becomes speckled or streaked rather than solid black. Juveniles may have a warm brown patterned back. The sexes have similar plumage, and overlapping size differences generally cannot establish sex confidently at a distance. Transitional plumage increases confusion with White-winged Tern and other species. Check head, rump and wing patterns along with bill and tail structure rather than relying on white cheeks alone. Habitat, food and behaviour It uses marshes, ponds, shallow lakes and freshwater wetlands, also appearing in suitable brackish and coastal habitats. It flies buoyantly back and forth above water and vegetation, taking insects and other invertebrates as well as small fish and crustaceans, sometimes making shallow dives. Its feeding does not always resemble the deeper plunge-diving of some marine terns. Water availability affects distribution: a flooded, vegetated area may provide feeding or nesting habitat, then lose that function when drained or cleared. Simply seeing a bird over a pool does not establish which role that site plays. Range and Arab occurrence The species occurs in separated populations across parts of Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia, with movements varying by population and water availability. In the Arab region, Lebanon’s 2026 guide describes a scarce passage migrant and rare, irregular summer breeder, recording nesting on an Assi River floodplain in 1995 and 1996. In contrast, Oman’s published official list describes abundant passage and winter occurrence. These differences rule out treating the species as a resident breeder throughout the Arab region, or interpreting all winter presence as late passage on the basis of Lebanon alone. In Kuwait, the local reference describes uncommon passage and scarce winter occurrence, especially at freshwater marshes around Jahra. Breeding and development It nests colonially on vegetation platforms over water or among aquatic plants. A scientific paper published in 2026 summarises breeding as a three-egg clutch with shared incubation of about 21 days. It reports approximately 19–21 days in the nest, followed by several weeks of parental care after flight begins. These values come from a European research context, not local measurements of every Arab population. Later parental contributions may differ: research on the studied populations records females leaving before care ends and males continuing. It is therefore misleading to imply that both parents always provide equal care until independence. November and responsible observation November in Oman falls within expected winter occurrence. A Lebanese observation should be interpreted against local and seasonal records without assuming new breeding. Watch from a pool margin, allowing birds to pass, and record flight style, feeding and plumage. Avoid entering the water or steering boats towards groups, and do not pursue resting birds for an open-wing photograph. Near any possible colony, distance is especially important: vegetation platforms and small chicks may be hard to see, and forcing them to move is not harmless simply because no immediate injury is visible. Conservation Its global category is Least Concern (LC), but local colonies remain vulnerable to drainage, disturbance and changes in water management. The Lebanon guide identifies recreational activities, drainage, illegal hunting and grazing at nesting sites among pressures, as well as avian influenza. Conservation requires aquatic vegetation, work scheduled away from breeding where it is confirmed, and quiet feeding and resting areas. Do not touch dead or sick birds; report their location to the appropriate authority from a safe distance without diagnosing the cause from appearance alone. articles.title: Woodlark
articles.body: Woodlark Lullula arborea — The voice of open woodland edges and grassy slopes Name and identity Woodlark is Lullula arborea, a member of Alaudidae within Passeriformes. The Lebanese guide uses the Arabic name Qubbarat al-ghab; Kuwaiti references also use Qubbarat al-ghabat. AviList 2026 recognises the same species in Lullula. Its name may suggest dense forest, but it is more closely associated with open ground interspersed with trees and shrubs, and with woodland edges. Such habitat combines feeding and nesting ground with elevated vegetation used for perching and singing. Identification It is a streaked brown lark with a short tail and broad pale eyebrows that meet across the back of the head. The crest is short and not always obvious; a dark mark bordered with white occurs at the front of the wing. Sexes share similar plumage. Juveniles look more spotted and scaled through pale feather edges; after complete moult, plumage pattern alone cannot determine age. Compared with Skylark, it has more compact proportions, a shorter tail and lacks the conspicuous white trailing wing edge. Crested Lark has a longer crest and different bill and proportions. Broad rounded wings and a short tail help confirm identification in flight. Habitat, food and behaviour Well-drained ground with short or patchy vegetation and scattered trees or shrubs is preferred. Habitats include woodland edges, clearings, pastures, slopes, small fields and some orchards and vineyards. Food is collected from the ground and low vegetation. Insects and spiders are important during breeding, with seeds prominent in autumn and winter; chicks receive small animal prey. The male is known for clear sequences of song given from a perch or during circling flight, and song may be heard beyond the main breeding period. Small groups may forage together in winter. Breeding and parental care The nest is placed on the ground beside a grass tussock or vegetation cover, with the female building a grass cup in a shallow hollow. BTO gives a typical clutch of three to five eggs, incubated by the female for about 14 days. Both parents feed the chicks, which generally leave at 11–13 days; flying ability may still be limited and care continues outside the nest. A further brood may follow. These are reference durations, whereas the Lebanese guide records egg laying from early April in mountain habitats. A young bird on the ground is not necessarily abandoned; observe from a distance rather than forcing it to move. Distribution and migration in the Arab region Its western Palearctic range extends from Europe into North Africa and parts of western Asia. The Lebanese guide describes it as a common breeding resident of open edges and rocky, grassy mountain habitats, with winter movements to lower elevations. A November observation may therefore reflect movement within the country rather than arrival from abroad. Some southern populations are resident, while northern populations migrate or move in response to conditions. Kuwait classifies it as a rare passage migrant and winter visitor. Lebanon’s “common resident” status should consequently not be extended to the Arabian Peninsula or to every wooded habitat. Ecological role and conservation AviList 2026 conservation data classify it globally as Least Concern, while local population status varies. Agricultural intensification, loss of vegetation structure or dense overgrowth of formerly open sites can remove suitable habitat. Ground nesting increases sensitivity to disturbance, trampling and operations that directly affect nests. Maintaining mosaics of open grassland and scattered trees, reducing pesticides and avoiding nesting areas are more appropriate than treating dense tree planting as a solution for every bird. Recording altitude and season during observations helps clarify local mountain movements. References AviList Core Team — AviList v2026, 20 October 2026.
